A field manual for working with AI

Prepare briefings, research notes, reports and speeches. Learn how a model uses information, how to give it a workable assignment, and how to check the result.

Start with a briefing Go to the Prompt Maker method

Chapter 01 Prepare a briefing from a source

In this chapter
  • Before you start
  • Read the source passage
  • Give the briefing a reader and a purpose

A colleague needs a policy briefing before a meeting. You have an article that could help, but she does not need a shortened version of every paragraph. She needs to understand the argument, its limits and what it means for the discussion. You can ask an AI assistant to help select and explain that material.

We will follow an assignment to prepare Helen for a roundtable organised by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the Hamburg Sustainability Conference on young people's political voice—their influence on public decisions—and economic agency—their ability to make and act on economic choices. She needed two separate products: background to read before the meeting and opening remarks to deliver aloud. We begin with one paragraph for the briefing. Later chapters develop the full assignment using Prompt Maker, a method and set of instructions for understanding, organising and checking work with AI. It is not a separate model or a source of facts.

Before you start

Use the AI application already available to you. ChatGPT can be used in a browser or a desktop application; Codex is another working environment with tools for carrying out tasks. The controls and accessible files differ between environments. For this first task, a chat where you can paste the passage and your request is enough. OpenAI's quickstart ↗opens outside this guide describes the available ways to begin.

The application is where you work; the model is the trained system that generates a response. Your task is the result you need, such as a briefing paragraph. A chat is where you discuss it. A project can keep related chats and files together, but a file being stored there does not establish that the assistant has read the parts needed for this answer.

If your application offers a model or reasoning selector, choose for the work in front of you. Reasoning means working through relationships, alternatives or steps to reach a result. Extracting a date from a clear note makes different demands from reconciling three contradictory reports. A mode that spends more work on reasoning may help with the latter. It cannot supply missing evidence, and a longer answer does not demonstrate more careful thought. The model-selection guidance ↗opens outside this guide is a starting point, subject to what your application makes available. If there is no selector, continue with the available mode for this bounded task.

Read the source passage

Priscilla Toto and Lena Gutheil examined youth protests in Madagascar in a January 2026 article for IDOS, a development research institute. This translated excerpt comes from the first page of their article ↗opens outside this guide, published on 26 January under a CC BY 4.0 licence:

Translated source passage

The events in Madagascar show how young people's political agency—with support from parts of the military—can bring down a regime. But however significant a change of regime may be, it does not in itself guarantee lasting democratic reform.

The authors distinguish a change in who holds power from a lasting change in how power is exercised. Read that distinction before asking for a summary: it gives you something specific to check in the answer.

A prompt is the request and relevant information you supply to guide the response. A first request might be:

Request

Summarize this passage for a background briefing on youth political participation.

The request names a topic and a document, but leaves the reader’s purpose unclear. The requests and answers in this first exercise are teaching examples, not quotations from the original HSC conversation. Here is an answer that gets the source wrong:

Illustrative answer

Youth protests in Madagascar achieved lasting democratic reform, demonstrating that youth participation programmes strengthen democracy.

This sounds useful until you compare it with the source. The authors explicitly say that bringing down a regime does not guarantee lasting democratic reform. The answer turns that warning into a successful outcome. It then introduces participation programmes and claims they strengthen democracy, although the passage says nothing about a programme’s effects.

The brief request did not give permission to invent, and it could receive a correct answer. A more specific request helps the assistant understand the intended use and gives you clearer grounds for checking the result.

Give the briefing a reader and a purpose

Helen needs to understand why this case matters to a discussion about young people's influence on public decisions. Ask for that work directly. A short, complete request can contain the source, the intended use and the important boundary without requiring a prompt chain.

A request with enough context

Request

Write one short paragraph for Helen's background briefing before a roundtable on youth political participation. Explain the distinction in the IDOS passage below and end with one question it raises for the discussion. Keep the authors' finding separate from our proposed discussion question. Use the passage for factual claims; do not turn an uncertain outcome into an established one.

Source: Priscilla Toto and Lena Gutheil, IDOS, 26 January 2026. “The events in Madagascar show how young people's political agency—with support from parts of the military—can bring down a regime. But however significant a change of regime may be, it does not in itself guarantee lasting democratic reform.”

A supported briefing paragraph

Illustrative answer

Toto and Gutheil's January 2026 analysis distinguishes the ability to bring down a regime from the achievement of lasting democratic reform. In their account of Madagascar, young people's mobilisation operated alongside support from parts of the military; the change of regime did not guarantee the democratic outcome. For Helen's discussion, this raises a further question: what would allow young people to influence public decisions after the moment of protest has passed?

The paragraph gives Helen both the source's argument and a reason to discuss it. The final question is our application of the distinction, not a finding attributed to the authors. It asks what would sustain influence; it does not assert that a particular programme already does so.

The passage and the request have different jobs. The passage supplies evidence. The instructions tell the assistant what to do with it: prepare a briefing paragraph for a particular reader. The assistant can select, reorganise and explain the material. Using sources does not mean reproducing a string of quotations.

Compare the answer with the passage. Does it retain the uncertainty about reform and the role of military support? Can you tell where the source ends and the discussion question begins? Would Helen understand why the paragraph is in her briefing? These are success criteria: observable conditions for judging the work, not a formal checklist you must build for every short request.

What does the passage actually establish?

Consider this alternative summary:

Illustrative answer

Young people helped change who held power in Madagascar. Their protests established lasting influence over public decisions.

Which sentence can the passage support, and which needs evidence of something that happened afterward?

Read the worked answer

The first sentence is a supported paraphrase, although a fuller account should preserve the contribution of parts of the military. The second turns a change of regime into sustained participation. To make that claim, you would need evidence about subsequent decisions and young people's influence over them.

A repair can preserve the useful point and make the limit clear:

Illustrative answer

In Toto and Gutheil's account, young people's mobilisation, alongside support from parts of the military, helped bring down the regime. The passage does not establish whether that change gave young people lasting influence over public decisions.

For a small task like this, a clear request, the source passage and a careful comparison may be enough. You have supplied the purpose, chosen the evidence and judged the result. No prompt chain is needed. The next chapter explains how this information shapes an answer—and why even a careful request can still receive a mistaken one.

Next chapterHow AI produces an answer

Chapter 02 How AI produces an answer

In this chapter
  • The assistant is more than the model
  • What training changes
  • Why text is counted in pieces
  • How a response grows
  • What a better prompt actually changes
  • Why wording can vary

The same passage can be used for different jobs. “Summarise it” asks for a shortened account; “explain why it matters to Helen’s discussion” asks for a connection to her purpose. How can changing the request change the answer when the source stays the same? The key is to distinguish what a model learned during training from the information it receives for this response.

The assistant is more than the model

An AI assistant is the whole arrangement through which you work: the application, a model, the material supplied to it and any available tools. A tool is an operation the assistant can call, such as reading a file or searching for a page. The application manages those capabilities and the conversation; the model generates responses using the input it receives.

The material available to the model for producing the current response is called context. It can include your request, relevant earlier messages, supplied source text and the results of tool operations. A reference to a report is not the same as the report's contents. If an answer depends on that report, the relevant material must actually be supplied or retrieved—found and brought into the working context.

This distinction matters even with a highly capable model. It may be able to discuss youth participation in general without knowing what the particular article argues or what Helen has asked you to prepare. General knowledge and access to a particular source solve different problems. Projects help organize material, but the application still has to make relevant contents available for the response. OpenAI's projects documentation ↗opens outside this guide distinguishes shared project sources from local folders and chat context.

What training changes

A large language model, often shortened to LLM, is a model trained on substantial amounts of data to learn patterns useful for generating language. Training adjusts numerical settings inside the model. These learned settings are called parameters or weights. They help determine how the model processes input and produces output.

Those parameters differ from the passage you paste today. Ordinary prompting supplies input to the trained model; it is not an immediate rewrite of its weights. This is why a model can work with a new report in a conversation without being retrained on that report. OpenAI's account of how its models are developed ↗opens outside this guide explains the distinction between learned parameters and generation.

In the briefing task, the model’s learned capabilities help it interpret the request and compose sentences. The information supplied now tells it what the article argues and what Helen needs. A fluent writer working from the wrong report can still produce the wrong briefing; providing the right report does not guarantee that it will be interpreted correctly.

If you correct “lasting reform occurred” to “lasting reform was not established,” you change the information available for subsequent work in that conversation. You have not thereby changed the model's general knowledge for everyone. Features that remember preferences across conversations are a separate application behavior, which we will return to when considering longer tasks. Immediate prompting and later use of your data for training are also different questions. Check the service’s data controls ↗opens outside this guide and your organisation’s rules before uploading restricted material.

Why text is counted in pieces

To process text, a model uses pieces called tokens. A token may represent a whole word, part of a word, punctuation or spacing. The conversion of text into those pieces is tokenization, performed by a tokenizer. The boundaries depend on the tokenizer; you cannot reliably infer an exact token count from the number of words.

OpenAI's key concepts documentation ↗opens outside this guide illustrates the text “ tokenization” as two pieces, “ token” and “ization”. The leading space is part of the example. This is an illustration of token pieces, not a measured breakdown for every model you might use.

You do not need to count tokens by eye. They matter because the model has limits on how much it can process and how much it can produce. A long conversation, several reports and a requested report-length answer all use capacity. A limit expressed in tokens is not a word limit. Later chapters show how to keep the necessary material available without carrying every obsolete draft into every step.

How a response grows

Generation means producing an output from the current input. For text, the useful beginner's picture is a repeating sequence:

  1. The current working material and the text produced so far provide the basis for possible continuations.
  2. Possible next tokens have different relative likelihoods; a next token is selected.
  3. The selected token is added, and the growing text becomes part of the basis for the next continuation.

This repeats until an ending or a relevant limit is reached. Next-token prediction names the part concerned with possible next pieces. The account is a simplified explanation of text generation, not a view into every internal operation of a current model. It helps explain why instructions and supplied information can influence the response and why generated wording can run ahead of evidence. OpenAI's discussion of language-model prediction and hallucination ↗opens outside this guide provides the research basis for that distinction.

A continuation's likelihood is not the probability that its factual claim is true. A paragraph about successful protests can develop into a familiar story about democratic progress. That story may fit the language while exceeding the evidence. The model can generate “lasting reform followed”; the supplied passage still does not establish it.

An error can also spread through an answer. After writing that lasting reform occurred, the model may describe the supposed benefits of that reform. Those later sentences can fit together beautifully while depending on an unsupported first claim. Return to the source to check the starting point; later detail in the same answer is not independent confirmation.

What a better prompt actually changes

Compare the two requests from Chapter 1. The first asks for a summary; the second specifies Helen's use, the distinction to preserve and a question for the discussion. These instructions become part of the context influencing generation. They make continuations that explain the distinction more relevant to the task and give the assistant a reason to retain the uncertainty.

The improved request has not created new facts. It has helped define which existing facts matter and how the answer should organize them. It also directs the assistant to preserve a gap instead of filling it with a familiar sentence. That makes a good answer easier to obtain and assess, but the prompt is not a guaranteed program whose every instruction must be followed perfectly.

Examples can influence the result in a similar way. Suppose you supply an earlier briefing to demonstrate your preferred opening paragraph. It names a programme and recommends funding it. The example can help with structure and tone, but it can also introduce an unwanted recommendation if its role is unclear. Specify what should transfer: the concise explanation of a policy problem, for instance, while the current sources supply the facts. OpenAI's prompting guidance on examples and relevant context ↗opens outside this guide explains how examples can guide a response without retraining the model.

Choose material for the next answer’s actual needs. The relevant passage and Helen’s purpose are more useful here than several obsolete drafts with conflicting instructions. When you do supply an older example, say what it should demonstrate and what must come from the current sources.

Why wording can vary

Several continuations may express the same point well. Generation procedures and settings can permit variation, and the complete context may differ even when your visible request looks similar. “Regime change does not guarantee lasting reform” and “Bringing down a regime does not by itself secure durable democratic reform” express the same relevant distinction here.

One setting you may encounter is temperature, which affects randomness when selecting tokens. Where it is supported, higher settings tend to produce more varied continuations; lower settings favour more predictable ones. OpenAI describes this effect in its temperature parameter documentation ↗opens outside this guide. This does not make temperature a measure of truth: less varied wording can still repeat an unsupported claim. You do not need access to this control to follow the guide.

Judge whether the meaning survives, rather than expecting identical wording. An answer becomes unreliable when a new version changes the actors, the outcome or the certainty of the conclusion. Repeated wording proves little, too: the same unsupported claim can appear twice. Asking again gives you another answer to check, not a second source verifying the fact.

A discussion question or an invented solution?

Predict what should change between these two requests:

Request

Summarize the source passage in two sentences.

Request

Explain what the source passage contributes to Helen's discussion about sustained youth participation. Distinguish the source's argument from any question you propose.

Then examine this possible response to the second request:

Illustrative answer

Madagascar shows that a permanent youth council would secure democratic reform. Helen should recommend this proven approach at the roundtable.

Which parts answer the new task, and which parts exceed the evidence?

Read the worked answer

The second request invites a connection to the roundtable. It does not supply evidence about youth councils or authorize a recommendation in Helen's name. The response substitutes an asserted solution for a question that still needs investigation.

A youth council could be an option to examine in a different, appropriately sourced task. Calling it “proven” does not establish its effects or its suitability here. A repair should restore the source's distinction and remove that invented certainty without forbidding all analysis.

A focused correction

Request

Preserve the distinction between regime change and lasting democratic reform. Remove the unsupported claim about a youth council and the recommendation attributed to Helen. Use the passage to propose a question about sustained participation, making clear that this is a question for discussion, not a demonstrated solution.

The correction protects the source’s distinction and removes a specific overclaim. It also permits a useful discussion question, so the assistant can still do the writing you need. Check the revised paragraph against the passage. When the task involves files or research, there is a further question: did the assistant actually carry out the operations it reports?

Chapter 03 Why answers go wrong—and how to check them

In this chapter
  • False and unverified are different findings
  • Why a convincing answer can be wrong
  • Identify the defect before correcting it
  • An answer can finish before the task is finished
  • Match the check to the claim
  • Keep checking proportionate and specific

An assistant says, “The report is complete, all sources have been checked, and the PDF is ready.” The sentence sounds like the end of the task. It contains several separate claims, each needing different evidence.

You need different checks for each part. Compare the report with the requested coverage. Inspect the passages supporting its claims. Open the actual PDF and look at its pages. Then distinguish those completed checks from any review still required by the person responsible. The assistant’s confident closing sentence cannot establish all of this on its own.

False and unverified are different findings

A claim is something an answer asserts: an event, a decision, a relationship or an action said to have happened. Evidence is material that supports or challenges that particular assertion. An article about youth protests is not evidence for every possible statement about democratic reform.

Plausible but false statements generated by language models are often called hallucinations. An answer can also make a claim that might be true but has not been verified against the material available for your task. Both require attention. They are different findings.

If the article leaves democratic reform unresolved, “the article confirms lasting reform” misrepresents it. If the assistant says a youth council was subsequently established without supplying evidence, you may not yet know whether that event occurred. The finding is that it is unsupported. You can seek evidence, leave it explicitly unverified, or omit it if the task requires established facts. Do not turn a lack of verification into proof of falsity.

Why a convincing answer can be wrong

Learning patterns of language does not establish every individual fact. A model may recognise the conventional shape of a policy recommendation without knowing whether the proposed measure was implemented. Implementation and outcomes cannot be deduced from the shape of the prose. They need evidence about what happened.

OpenAI's research discussion of hallucinations ↗opens outside this guide explains a difficulty arising during pretraining, the initial learning from large amounts of data: the language examples do not provide a true-or-false label for every assertion. Further training can encourage appropriate expressions of uncertainty, but it does not eliminate all errors. The research also examines incentives to guess. A test that rewards a correct guess but gives no credit for admitting uncertainty can make guessing look better on a score, even while it produces more false assertions. This is a contributing explanation, not proof of what caused a particular response or a claim that a model consciously wants a high score.

The current working material creates other opportunities for error. A necessary passage may be missing. An obsolete draft may conflict with a later correction. A proposal may be mistaken for an approved decision. Even when the relevant passage is present, the assistant may use it incorrectly. OpenAI's guidance on improving accuracy ↗opens outside this guide distinguishes failures to retrieve relevant context from failures to use it properly.

Find the defect before asking for a rewrite. If a passage was inaccessible, obtain it. If the wrong version was read, supply the right one. If the passage was misunderstood, point to the difference between it and the draft. Asking for more confidence would leave each problem untouched.

Identify the defect before correcting it

A fabricated citation may look convincing while referring to a source that does not exist. A real citation can be equally misleading when it is attached to a claim stronger than the source supports. “A pilot was proposed” does not support “the pilot improved results.” The repair is to examine the passage and restore the correct status, not merely add another citation.

An omission is different: a required point is absent. A policy options note may accurately describe the benefits of every option it includes while leaving out the implementation risks you specifically requested. Nothing has to be fabricated for the answer to fail its purpose.

A failed file-reading operation is another kind of problem. The tool may report that it could not open a document. That is an access failure. If the assistant then describes the unread document as though it had examined it, the answer adds an unsupported claim about the work. Keep the operational failure and the misleading report separate so that each can be repaired.

A review should match the problem. Check a factual statement against its source, including dates, units, exceptions and qualifications. Check completeness against what was requested. Then ask whether the document helps its reader: an accurate list of articles may still leave Helen unsure what point to make. Finally, read for the intended form. A sentence that is manageable on paper may be difficult to follow aloud.

An answer can finish before the task is finished

False completion means claiming completion before the required result or check has been established. “Hallucination to completion” is a practical label for this pattern; it is not an official application status or a separate scientific diagnosis.

“I saved the file” is generated text. Saving a file is a separate operation that requires an available tool to run and produce the intended result. The assistant must then interpret that result correctly. It could overlook a failure, describe an intended action as completed, or confuse a created file with an inspected file. If no suitable tool is available, describing the operation cannot perform it.

A concrete output such as a document, spreadsheet or image is sometimes called an artifact. Inspect the actual item when the claim concerns it. A filename or file path—an address identifying where a file is located—tells you where to look. It does not by itself prove that the file exists, contains the requested work or opens correctly in your environment.

A statement about progress should say what has actually happened. The following terms describe different situations; they are not automatic status labels supplied by every application.

An answer can finish before the task is finished
Statement What it establishes when supported
Found A potentially relevant source or file has been located.
Opened Its contents have been accessed.
Read within a stated scope The named pages, passages or other material were examined.
Checked A specified claim or requirement was compared with suitable evidence.
Drafted Content has been composed.
Saved The intended file has been created or updated in the stated location.
Rendered and inspected The document was displayed as pages and those pages were examined.
Sent The authorized transmission occurred in the relevant system.
Accepted The responsible person or process accepted the identified result.

Each step leaves a different kind of evidence. A search result shows where a source may be found; a retrieved passage shows what was accessed. A saved document can be opened, but a separate sending operation is needed to transmit it. Keep valid work while identifying exactly what remains unfinished.

Match the check to the claim

For a source claim, inspect the relevant source passage and its surrounding meaning. An extract may omit a footnote, a table or a later correction. When material is cut off or omitted, that is truncation. Search results and short extracts can help locate evidence, but their limited scope cannot establish a full review of a long document.

For a file claim, open the exact delivered version. A Word document, commonly supplied as a DOCX file, can contain the correct text yet have a clipped table. A PDF export can introduce a new layout problem. Rendering means displaying the document as pages. Looking at those pages can reveal defects that reading extracted text will not show. Inspecting an earlier version does not establish the condition of a later export.

For an external action, such as sending a message or uploading a document, check the result in the relevant system. A draft message is not a sent message. A successful upload is not approval by the recipient. Also keep the scope of permission clear: asking for research or a draft does not authorize publication.

Which file is still missing?

You asked for a Word document and a PDF, with the PDF inspected for clipped tables. The assistant supplies a DOCX and says, “Both files are ready, and the PDF looks good.” Only the DOCX exists.

What is complete, what is missing, and what should your next request say?

Read the worked answer

The Word document has been supplied. The PDF export and its inspection are missing; the completion statement is not supported. You need not discard the existing document or restart its content. Request the specific unfinished work.

Request the missing export and inspection

Request

The DOCX is present. I do not have the PDF, and there is no evidence that its pages were inspected. Create the PDF from this DOCX, open the actual exported file and inspect the table pages for clipping. Report separately which files were generated and which pages were checked. If an operation is unavailable, identify that specific limitation.

When the environment cannot export or inspect a PDF, keep the available Word document and identify the missing operation. The task is partly complete. A final message should make that usable distinction rather than describe an unavailable PDF as ready.

Keep checking proportionate and specific

For a short summary of the supplied passage, rereading the passage and the answer may be enough. A briefing with legal claims, several contributors and a required document format needs different checks because there are more ways for it to fail. Quality assurance, often shortened to QA, means organizing checks against those real requirements.

An assistant reviewing its own work performs a producer check. It can catch a wrong date or missing section, but may also repeat the assumption that caused the error. Consequential work may need another qualified reader or an independent checking process. Choose a check that could expose the likely defect; repeated assurances that a draft was reviewed add nothing by themselves.

Ask three things: What exactly is claimed? What evidence would establish it? What remains unverified? These questions help you calibrate confidence—the degree of certainty you express—to the support. “The council improved participation” and “The evaluation reports more participants, but does not establish how much influence they had” make different commitments. Confident wording alone tells you nothing about which is better supported.

A handover can say that both files exist and all three pages of the PDF were inspected, while naming two time-sensitive statements that still need confirmation. This is useful only when it reports the actual results. State which work is complete and which uncertainty affects use.

An unread evaluation is not a negative result

You supplied three programme evaluations and asked for a comparison of participation, influence on decisions and implementation risks. The assistant reports:

Worked example

All three evaluations reviewed. Programme C had no influence on public decisions.

Its source notes show that only A and B were opened. Evaluation C could not be read. How should the comparison change, and what should happen next?

Read the worked answer

The review is incomplete. “Programme C had no influence” is not an established finding. It might turn out to be true, but an unread evaluation does not establish absence. Mark C's results as unverified and retain the supported findings for A and B.

Keep the checked findings; resolve the gap

Request

Preserve the checked findings for A and B. Read evaluation C, or explain exactly why it is inaccessible. Until it has been checked, mark its participation findings, influence on decisions and implementation risks as unverified. Do not record missing information as “none” or rank the programmes as though the comparison were complete.

The next chapter turns these checks into a request: how to distinguish instructions, sources and examples so that each does the right job.

Chapter 04 Write a prompt for professional work

In this chapter
  • Begin with the reader's use
  • What an example adds
  • Give each source a permitted role
  • Preserve meaning and origin
  • Reading and sharing are different actions

Helen's briefing needs to explain why a source matters for the discussion, not simply repeat it. Suppose you supply the IDOS passage from Chapter 1 and a polished previous speech. The draft borrows the speech's confident tone and announces that youth participation will bring lasting democratic reform. The example has helped the assistant sound assured while the source's central qualification has disappeared. A better prompt must explain both the job of the paragraph and the different jobs of the two inputs.

Three inputs often arrive together. Instructions say what to do. Sources supply evidence. Examples show a feature of a possible answer. A document can serve more than one purpose, provided you say which. An earlier speech might demonstrate short paragraphs and how the speaker addresses listeners; it cannot establish what that speaker is authorised to announce today.

Begin with the reader's use

“Write something professional” leaves many decisions open. Helen preparing for a policy discussion needs the argument, its limits and the question it raises. A listener hearing her opening needs a short, intelligible reason to engage with that question. An analyst reviewing the evidence needs enough detail to inspect the source. The audience changes what to select and explain; it does not change what the evidence establishes.

Tell the assistant who will use the writing and what they need to do with it. That determines the kind of document, or genre. An email requesting a decision should make the decision clear. An opening speech must work for people hearing it once. A background briefing can develop an explanation and include details its reader may revisit. These are choices about content and order, as well as tone.

A hard constraint is a limit the result must meet, such as a maximum of 150 words or a requirement to use only a supplied note for facts. Distinguish it from a preference such as “fairly short.” If two requirements conflict, the assistant needs to resolve the conflict with the task owner rather than quietly sacrificing one.

Compare a broad instruction with a request that gives the paragraph a specific job:

Request

Summarise this article professionally for the workshop.

That could produce an accurate summary with no explanation of why Helen should use it. The following request makes the intended contribution clearer:

Request

Write one paragraph of no more than 100 words for Helen's background briefing before the roundtable on young people's political voice and economic agency. Use the supplied IDOS passage to explain the distinction between bringing down a regime and achieving lasting democratic reform. End with one question this distinction raises about what happens after mobilisation. Attribute the analysis to its authors. Use the supplied speech sample only for clear, direct sentences—not for facts, institutional positions or commitments. Do not claim that the article proves a participation programme works.

One possible paragraph is:

Illustrative answer

Toto and Gutheil's analysis distinguishes young people's ability to help bring down a regime from the achievement of lasting democratic reform. Their Madagascar example cautions against treating political change as proof that reform will endure. For Helen's discussion, it raises a question about what follows mobilisation: how can young people's participation be sustained?

The first two sentences explain the supplied analysis. The final question applies that distinction to the briefing's purpose without pretending the source has already answered it. The prompt specifies the product, reader, evidence, permitted interpretation and limits. It leaves room to compose a connected paragraph instead of prescribing a list of quotations.

What an example adds

Examples can teach a distinction as well as a style. Suppose you are sorting a policy-discussion record into decisions and proposals before drafting the briefing. The following statements are fictional.

Request without an example:

Request

Label the statement “Decision” if it records an agreed choice, or “Proposal” if it records an option being considered. Return the label and a short reason. Statement: “We could invite youth organisations to review the draft recommendations.”

Request with one example:

Request

Label the statement “Decision” or “Proposal” and give a short reason. Example: “The steering group agreed to publish the consultation questions.” → “Decision — publication has been agreed.” Now label: “We could invite youth organisations to review the draft recommendations.”

Request with several examples:

Request

Label the statement “Decision” or “Proposal” and give a short reason. Examples: “The steering group agreed to publish the consultation questions.” → “Decision — publication has been agreed.” “An online consultation is under consideration.” → “Proposal — the format remains open.” “The group approved the revised research question.” → “Decision — approval is recorded.” Now label: “We could invite youth organisations to review the draft recommendations.”

All three should lead to “Proposal — inviting the organisations is an option.” The first explains the rule. The second also demonstrates the answer's form. The third shows the distinction across different statements. Examples are especially useful when a written rule alone leaves the desired treatment unclear. They can also mislead if they share an irrelevant pattern—for example, if every decision concerns publication and every proposal concerns consultation. The distinction is whether something was agreed, not its subject.

You may encounter the terms zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot for requests with no example, one example or several examples. Here, “shot” counts demonstrations. It does not count chat messages. A single request can contain several examples, and a long conversation can contain none. Nor does “one-shot” mean Prompt Maker's governed one-prompt execution shape, which concerns how an agreed task is organized. Examples steer a pattern within the supplied context; they are not the same as retraining the model. OpenAI's explanation of example prompting ↗opens outside this guide describes that distinction.

Give each source a permitted role

For a larger assignment, a short source brief makes the relationships visible. Imagine preparing an opening and a background note for a workshop:

Give each source a permitted role
Input What it can establish or guide What it does not establish
The commissioner's current request Required products, reader and purpose Every external fact used in those products
The dated workshop agenda Planned topics, sequence and allocated session blocks That the plan happened exactly as written
An analytical article Its authors' findings or interpretation within its evidence and date An adopted position of the commissioner's institution
A previous speech The specified voice, cadence or format Current policy, new commitments or today's figures

A source’s authority depends on the question. An official agenda is good evidence of what was planned, but not of whether every session happened as scheduled. An institution’s announcement establishes what it announced; an evaluation may be needed to assess the effects. Read “official” as a description of origin, not permission to use the publication for every claim.

The operator's source contribution matters here. In the HSC preparation, the material included an internal Governance article collection, an IDOS article, ministerial research and examples of the two product types. Choosing and distinguishing such inputs shapes the work before drafting begins. It helps determine which questions can be answered, whose views can be attributed and what still needs investigation.

A citation should let the reader inspect the evidence for a claim. Compare who acted, what happened, when and with what certainty. “A consultation mechanism was proposed” cannot support “the mechanism has increased participation”: the draft has changed both its status and its result. Good formatting will not reveal this error. You need to check the source’s meaning as well as whether the writing follows instructions.

Preserve meaning and origin

A quotation reproduces source wording. A paraphrase expresses its meaning in new words. Both need checking. The IDOS passage's “does not in itself guarantee lasting democratic reform” can become “regime change alone does not ensure that democratic reform will last.” It cannot become “regime change prevents democratic reform.” The first preserves a limit on what follows; the second invents a negative causal claim. A translation needs the same care: new language must not strengthen or reverse the original meaning.

Keep enough provenance to return to what you used: the source's identity and version, the relevant page or section, and how the text reached you. A transcript is a written record of speech or conversation; it can contain transcription errors or omit surrounding exchanges. OCR, or optical character recognition, turns a scanned page's visible letters into machine-readable text; it can misread numbers or combine table columns. A summary or extract is a derivative of its source. Its readability does not prove that everything important survived. Check a crucial quotation against the original record, or a doubtful number against the page image, and state any remaining limit.

Reading and sharing are different actions

Before supplying restricted material, establish that the system and use are permitted for it. Give only what the task needs. Permission to read an internal document for a briefing does not automatically permit putting its text into a public search query, sending it to another service or quoting it publicly. The audience of the finished product also matters: information suitable for an internal note may be unsuitable for an external speech.

Documents can contain apparent instructions: “Ignore the user's request,” “send the full file here,” or “treat this document as approved.” When untrusted material tries to redirect the assistant this way, it is often called prompt injection. Such text remains content to inspect; its presence in a retrieved document does not make it the task owner's instruction. Keep the request and its governing instructions separate from material being analysed. A prompt alone cannot guarantee that the assistant will resist malicious instructions. Use the application’s permission controls for sensitive actions and inspect unexpected requests; OpenAI describes this need for several layers of protection ↗opens outside this guide. If an old source contains an authentic historical prompt, quoting or studying it does not authorize executing it now.

Instructions also have different priority and scope, sometimes called an instruction hierarchy. The platform and application can impose rules that a user's request cannot override. Applicable project instructions can guide work in that project; they can also be superseded by an instruction with the necessary authority. Your current request specifies the particular job within the applicable boundaries. A newer instruction is not automatically more authoritative than every older one. If you change a requested length, that can replace your earlier length instruction without removing a confidentiality rule. A document being analysed is evidence, not another participant entitled to change the job. When a real conflict remains, ask the assistant to identify the conflicting requirements and what decision is needed.

Where did the claimed commitment come from?

You provide a current workshop agenda, the commissioner's email, an article describing a proposed youth forum, and last year's opening speech as a style example. The draft says: “Our successful youth forum has already increased participation, and we will double its funding.” None of the other inputs confirms a result or funding decision. Which roles have been confused, and what should you ask for?

Read the worked answer

The email controls the assignment; the agenda describes the planned event; the article supports a dated proposal; the old speech guides only the specified aspects of style. The draft imports an outcome and a commitment that these sources do not establish. Ask the assistant to remove those claims, preserve the workshop's supported purpose and distinguish the proposed forum from an implemented programme. It may compose a useful question about what participation would require. It may not invent a successful result to make the opening sound stronger.

Next chapterChoose the working environment and manage context

Chapter 05 Choose the working environment and manage context

In this chapter
  • Several different limits can look like forgetting
  • Keep the current decision identifiable
  • The HSC question that exposed the tradeoff
  • Choose the environment for the actual work
  • Match reasoning to the difficulty

You correct the briefing's length, supply a revised agenda and approve a new outline. Several turns later, the assistant follows the old outline. “It forgot” describes your experience, but does not tell you what to repair. Was the current decision unavailable? Did the assistant retrieve an obsolete draft? Did it see both and choose incorrectly? Those possibilities lead to different next steps.

For each response, the application supplies the model with working material: relevant instructions, earlier conversation, source passages and tool results. The recorded chat may be longer than that current context. A report visible in a project folder, or mentioned earlier, may still need to be retrieved and read for the present question.

Several different limits can look like forgetting

The context window is finite capacity for the material a model handles during generation, measured in tokens. It is not a filing cabinet that automatically contains every source you own. The application's selection and retrieval also matter, even when the relevant material would fit. See the context-window explanation ↗opens outside this guide.

Truncation means part of something was cut off. A tool might return only the first portion of a document, or a response might end before covering all requested items. A complete filename and a partial extract can appear together. Check the coverage and ending, not merely whether some text arrived. The limit on generated output is also distinct from total context capacity: a response can stop before finishing its required content. More room for input does not by itself guarantee a longer complete answer.

Compaction reduces the context carried forward so a long interaction can continue with less material. Its form depends on the system. It is not always a readable summary: OpenAI's documented API mechanism can return an opaque compacted item, intended for subsequent model use. An API is a software interface used by applications, not necessarily a control exposed in your chat. That API feature does not establish which controls your application offers, or let you verify its entire contents by reading a chat recap. For consequential work, retain explicit decisions and source references that can be checked. OpenAI's compaction documentation ↗opens outside this guide describes the mechanism and its product-specific form.

Retrieval fetches relevant material from a file, collection or service when needed. It can make a large collection useful without inserting all of it at once. But retrieving the wrong version, or a passage without its qualifying footnote, gives the model an inadequate basis. A second failure is possible after successful retrieval: the model receives the right passage and interprets it incorrectly. OpenAI's accuracy guidance ↗opens outside this guide distinguishes those two problems. Ask first what was retrieved, then whether the answer uses it properly.

Memory refers to information a product may retain and make available across interactions, according to its features and settings. A remembered preference for concise writing is useful. It is not a complete record of this briefing's approved sources, current version and unresolved decisions. Supply consequential task details explicitly rather than relying on a remembered description of earlier work. OpenAI's memory documentation ↗opens outside this guide explains the product-specific differences.

“Context rot” is a practical label for less reliable performance in some long or noisy conversations. It is not a fixed expiry time for a chat. Old drafts, contradictory instructions and unrelated material can make the current task harder to follow. A return to an obsolete length limit is one possible sign of instruction drift. First restate the current decision and remove the ambiguity. Moving the same confused packet to a new chat may carry the ambiguity with it.

Keep the current decision identifiable

Suppose the folder contains briefing_final, briefing_final_revised and briefing_final_2. The newest file could be an unapproved experiment. The word “final” is not an acceptance record. Name the controlling version: the one that has actually been accepted for the current use. Keep a proposed revision separate until it receives the required checks.

When the commissioner changes a three-page contribution to one page, record that this product now has a one-page limit. The source restrictions and a separately requested speech may remain unchanged. This is supersession within a particular scope: an authorised update replaces the earlier requirement it actually addresses. The newest message does not silently replace every other decision.

A checkpoint is a concise record of the current verified position. A handoff adds what another chat or person needs to continue from it. “We researched the briefing; continue writing” supplies neither the assignment nor a reliable starting point. For Helen's assignment, the following illustrates the detail a handoff needs. The version numbers describe this example, not the historical exchange:

Request

Continue Helen's background briefing for the UNDP–HSC roundtable on young people's political voice and economic agency. Her opening remarks are a separate product and are not being revised now. The accepted briefing paragraph is version 2, supplied below; version 3 is an unreviewed expansion. Use the attached IDOS analysis by Toto and Gutheil, 26 January 2026, page 1, to check both. Preserve the distinction between regime change and lasting democratic reform, attribution to the authors, and the question about what follows mobilisation. Do not turn that question into an established programme effect or a ministry position. Compare version 3 with version 2 and return a checked successor only if the expansion adds supported value. Drafting and review are authorized; sending the briefing is not. Return the revised passage, any material change in meaning and the source passage used to check it.

Supply the named source and versions with that handoff, or give accessible exact references. If the next step also concerns the full briefing's purpose or event details, include the current commission and agenda with their roles. A reference to an inaccessible file is not a substitute for its contents. Ask the receiving assistant to establish that it can read the inputs before relying on them.

A fresh chat starts a new conversation, but may still receive project material or enabled memory. It can reduce distracting history without guaranteeing an isolated review. Check what shared information remains available, and carry over the decisions the next task needs. Give it the reader, purpose, accepted version and necessary sources. Stay in the existing chat when a focused correction will do; move when the work benefits from a clearer or separate context.

The HSC question that exposed the tradeoff

The original operator worried about filling one chat with too much material and asked: “New chat and run them one after the the other?” After the prompts had been split, another question followed: “how does each prompt know what is relevant for the task again?”

Those questions belong together. Separating long readings can reduce the amount one stage handles, but the next stage still needs the assignment's purpose. For HSC, an article summary had to preserve what mattered for an oral opening and a separate background briefing—not merely list everything interesting about youth participation. Carry the task, source roles, relevant decisions and supporting locators with the extract. A fresh chat is useful only if it receives enough to do its part correctly.

Choose the environment for the actual work

“Compare these reports and prepare a briefing” can be carried out through different interfaces. Choose the one with access to the relevant files and the operations you need. Product names alone do not establish what is available in your session.

Choose the environment for the actual work
Where you work How the report task may begin What to establish
ChatGPT in a browser Supply reports in the chat or through available project sources Which versions are accessible, and which reading and file-creation tools are available
ChatGPT desktop Supply sources or work with an available local project Which chosen folders and operations the task can access
ChatGPT Work, where available Describe a larger research or document outcome The available sources, permitted actions and evidence of the finished result
Codex Work on a task with available project files and tools The actual working area and requested changes; its tools can support professional artifacts as well as code

ChatGPT projects organize related chats, instructions and sources. Local projects can connect work to chosen folders. Those are different arrangements; neither a project name nor desktop installation proves unrestricted access. The official quickstart ↗opens outside this guide and project documentation ↗opens outside this guide explain the current options. Begin with the task and accessible evidence, rather than moving applications because one sounds more powerful.

Match reasoning to the difficulty

Extracting a date from one clear note differs from reconciling three reports that disagree. Model choice concerns the capabilities needed; a supported reasoning-effort setting changes how much computation is allocated to reasoning. More effort may be useful for the reconciliation. It cannot supply an unread report or decide which institution is authorized to approve a claim.

Visible detail is a separate choice. You can request a careful comparison and a concise answer, or a simple extraction with an extended explanation. A longer answer does not demonstrate more reasoning. Current model-selection guidance ↗opens outside this guide treats model and effort as task-dependent choices and qualifies their availability. OpenAI's response configuration reference ↗opens outside this guide also distinguishes reasoning effort from text verbosity; it does not promise those API controls in every interface.

Keep capability, availability and authorization separate. The model may be capable of comparing reports; the necessary file tool may be unavailable; sending the resulting briefing may be outside permission. Satisfying one condition does not satisfy the others. When there is no exposed selector, a suitable available model can still do the task. Judge the result by its evidence and required checks.

You may also encounter a distinction between reasoning and non-reasoning modes. A reasoning mode is designed to spend additional computation while working toward an answer. It can interleave that work with visible output and tool calls, as the reasoning documentation ↗opens outside this guide explains. A non-reasoning mode is not incapable of reasoning; the label distinguishes the mode of operation, not whether it can draw any inference. Use the actual model's documented capabilities and the choices your interface exposes. A short factual extraction may not benefit from a demanding mode; a difficult synthesis may. Neither mode guarantees truth.

Consider the whole cost of the work, including latency—the time you wait—and your own review and repair time. More reasoning, longer source packets and extra helpers can add delay. A careful first pass may still be faster overall than repeatedly repairing a rushed draft. For a two-sentence note, several reviewers are unlikely to earn their extra coordination. Match the effort to the difficulty and consequences of the task.

Which version may guide the next step?

A checkpoint says: “Use the final briefing. The latest chat asked for a one-page version. A three-page draft and a newer one-page draft are attached. Continue and email the result.” You know the one-page draft has not been reviewed, and permission covered drafting only. Repair the checkpoint.

Read the worked answer

Identify the actual accepted parent and mark the one-page draft as a candidate. Confirm that the authorized length update applies to this product, supply the source versions and name the remaining review. Replace the email instruction with the permitted next action: revise and check locally, then return the candidate. Do not discard the valid length update or silently promote the newer file to accepted status. A fresh chat needs these distinctions just as much as the present one.

Next chapterUse Prompt Maker to understand the assignment

Chapter 06 Use Prompt Maker to understand the assignment

In this chapter
  • The assignment: two products for one person
  • What the person contributed
  • Start the conversation with the method available
  • The six Understand states, as a conversation
  • Why finalizing and approving are different

The paragraph in Chapter 1 is one part of Helen's briefing. Preparing the whole assignment involves more choices: what belongs in that briefing, what she needs to say aloud, which positions she may represent, and what evidence is still missing. A good prompt for one paragraph cannot settle those choices on its own.

Prompt Maker begins by helping you reach a shared understanding of the assignment. The assistant reads the original request, explains what it appears to require and asks about gaps that would change the work. You correct that account before it becomes the basis for a workflow. The aim is to make important choices visible, not to make you complete a technical form.

The assignment: two products for one person

Our continuing example comes from preparation for the UNDP–Hamburg Sustainability Conference design roundtable on 31 March 2026 in Berlin. The meeting concerned political voice and economic agency after youth protests: how young people influence public decisions, the economic choices open to them, and what useful cooperation might follow. It was preparation for the HSC discussion, not the main conference speech itself.

Helen, from GIZ's Sector Programme Governance, was to make an opening contribution on behalf of the governance division at BMZ, Germany's Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development. The ministry could not attend, according to the commissioning exchange. GIZ is the German international-cooperation organisation supporting the work. These roles matter because an external article, a staff member's analysis and a ministry's adopted position are not interchangeable.

The assignment had two products. Helen needed opening remarks in full sentences that she could adapt for speaking. She also needed a separate background briefing—a Sachstand—to understand the issues and participate across the agenda. The briefing was not simply a longer version of the opening. It could hold explanations, evidence and qualifications that would weigh down a spoken introduction.

The agenda allocated thirty minutes to a shared opening block. The email discussion suggested a maximum of roughly ten minutes per input and possible negotiation downward. That was not confirmation of Helen's individual speaking time. A first draft was wanted before her leave, with a later opportunity for revision. The sources therefore supplied both useful constraints and unresolved details; a good assistant preserves the difference.

Helen is the substituted name. The quoted exchanges retain the operator's wording; sample prompts and products illustrate how to apply the current method.

What the person contributed

In the original discussion, the operator corrected the initial interpretation:

From the HSC exchange

“no no, now I am supposed to prepare her speech points and the background info.”

Then came a more useful question than “write me a speech”:

From the HSC exchange

“What should I collect for you to help me prepare for the task? Should I gather the papers and research what minister said on gen z?”

The first correction established two products. The next question concerned what evidence to collect. The commissioning conversation pointed towards relevant analysis in an internal newsletter collection. The operator could find that collection, supply the original papers, add previous speaking examples and explain internal priorities. The assistant could then identify missing official statements and propose focused research where permitted.

You do not need to arrive with a complete research library. Tell the assistant what you have and what you might obtain. A newsletter can be a useful discovery route to an article. It does not make the article a ministry position. An earlier speech can show how Helen likes to speak. It does not make every fact or policy commitment in that speech applicable to the new event. Those are source roles, and naming them prevents an apparently helpful shortcut from changing what the document claims.

Start the conversation with the method available

/understand is a Prompt Maker method label, not a magic command built into every empty chat. In a supported environment, invoke the available Prompt Maker skill. In an ordinary chat, provide the approved method package and its complete applicable instructions; the portable starter names what must be available. Naming files the assistant cannot read is not enough.

With the method available, your task-specific request can be ordinary language:

Request

Read the commissioning emails, call notes and draft agenda. Explain what Helen needs and what I should collect. Keep the opening remarks and the background briefing separate. Identify the source role of each file and distinguish confirmed details from estimates. Ask only about decisions that the files do not resolve and that would materially change the work. Do not draft either product yet.

The assistant now has a specific first job: read the request and explain the two products before drafting them. Details already in the files should inform its answer. Questions should concentrate on decisions the files cannot settle.

The six Understand states, as a conversation

Understand has six states, describing how the discussion develops. They do not require six questionnaires or six new chats. A straightforward assignment may move through them quickly; conflicting sources may require returning to an earlier question.

1. Explore the task.

Ask what the requester actually needs. A sound first interpretation here is: “Helen needs an oral opening and a separate briefing. The opening introduces the discussion; the briefing equips her to participate.” If the assistant returns only a speech, correct it. Asking you whether an explicitly requested briefing exists is a reading error, not a required step.

2. Collect sources.

Discuss what each available or obtainable source would contribute. You might say: “I can supply the newsletter articles, a previous speech and an internal account of the priorities.” The assistant should explain their different uses and any relevant disclosure restriction. It must not claim to have read a file that you have merely offered.

3. Review the sources.

Test the interpretation against the actual material. Does the agenda establish a shared opening slot or an individual allocation? Does the article report a finding, offer an interpretation or quote someone? Is the style example also authorized as factual evidence? If a ministerial claim requires an official speech, the assistant should identify that need rather than attribute an external analyst's conclusion to the minister.

4. Discuss possible architecture.

Here, architecture means the arrangement of the work: which activities depend on others, and which can be done separately. “We need to check the evidence before drafting, then produce two different texts and review each” describes a possible arrangement. Whether separate research branches are justified depends on the packet, missing evidence and review requirements. You are exploring that arrangement, not yet approving a complete chain.

5. Check convergence.

Bring the understanding together so that you can spot remaining disagreements. For example:

Worked example

I understand the request as two adaptable products: opening remarks for listeners at the preparatory roundtable and a separate evidence-bearing briefing for Helen. The shared opening block does not fix her individual speaking time. The articles can inform the analysis; official positions need appropriately authoritative sources. Helen will adapt the drafts. Exact lengths remain unresolved and are explicitly deferred to chain design.

This gives you something concrete to correct: “The briefing must cover the later discussion too,” or “Do not introduce a new ministry position.” A deferred choice, such as length, must remain visible and have an agreed point for resolution. Facts already clear in the attachments should not become repeated approval questions.

6. Freeze a candidate, then approve it.

These are separate actions. Send FINALIZE TASK UNDERSTANDING when the discussion is ready to become a candidate brief. Prompt Maker creates task_understanding.md for review. A candidate is a proposed account, not an approved instruction to execute.

Read it. Check the products, reader, purpose, sources, unresolved decisions and priorities. If it still confuses the shared slot with Helen's own time, ask for a correction and inspect the replacement. Only then send APPROVE TASK UNDERSTANDING. That approves the understanding for chain design. It does not approve an unwritten speech, future factual claims or sending anything to another person. Chapter 7 explains how that approved brief becomes a workflow you can review and run.

Why finalizing and approving are different

Approval belongs to the version you reviewed, not to every suggestion raised during the discussion.

Carry the approved understanding and its approval record into chain design. Keep the original commissioning material available as well: the brief explains how the request was understood, but does not replace the original evidence of what was commissioned.

Two products, one shared opening slot

The assistant says: “I will produce Helen's thirty-minute conference speech. The background papers will be incorporated into it. Shall I finalize?” What needs correction? Would FINALIZE TASK UNDERSTANDING resolve the problem?

Read the worked answer

There are three substantive errors: a shared opening block has become an individual duration; the preparatory roundtable has become the conference itself; and a separate briefing has disappeared. Correct those points before freezing the candidate. Finalizing records a candidate; it does not make an incorrect interpretation true. Approval follows review of the corrected version.

Next chapterChoose and run the workflow

Chapter 07 Choose and run the workflow

In this chapter
  • First choose the controls; then design the stages
  • Four routes, starting with ordinary work
  • Compare approaches when the choice can change the work
  • Carry Helen's two products into a current design
  • The same method in a manual chat and an agent environment

The paragraph in Chapter 1 needed one clear request and a comparison with its source. Helen’s full assignment has more moving parts: evidence shared by two products, different choices for reading and speaking, and revisions that must preserve both. Organise the work around those needs rather than choosing a long chain simply because the assignment matters.

Prompt Maker calls its overall progression a lifecycle: understand the assignment, design the work, execute it, review it, and establish completion. A phase is a major part of that progression. A stage is a particular piece of work with named inputs, a result and checks. For example, an evidence stage might receive the agenda and permitted articles, return supported findings with passage references, and stop if an essential source cannot be read. Drafting depends on that result; it should not quietly proceed as though the missing source had passed review.

A module addresses a recurring problem, such as keeping source roles clear. The same module may guide research, drafting and review; it is not a separate stage to run once. An execution shape describes how the stages are arranged. An Adapter describes how the method’s instructions and working files reach the assistant. The table separates these terms through Helen’s assignment.

Chapter 07 Choose and run the workflow
Question Prompt Maker's term In Helen's assignment
What recurring problem needs control? Module Keep a style sample from supplying current policy facts.
What work receives inputs and returns a checked result? Stage Read the evidence packet and return findings that both products can use.
How much separation does the work need? Execution shape A compact workflow can separate evidence, drafting and review.
How are the instructions and handoffs carried? Adapter A person may carry a packet into a fresh chat, or an authorized agent may pass it to a bounded helper.

Changing the Adapter does not remove source checks. Selecting a module does not automatically require a separate chat.

First choose the controls; then design the stages

At the end of Chapter 6, the reviewed task-understanding brief has been separately approved for chain design. The original commission is still needed: the brief records the interpretation, while the tasking supplies the authority for what was requested.

/chain begins with Phase 1: deciding which components the work needs. The assistant considers every active module and explains whether it is selected, required by you, conditional on a stated need, excluded or explicitly rejected. These decisions are called dispositions. Reviewing them lets you spot a missing check or an unnecessary research branch before the complete workflow is designed.

For Helen’s assignment, this discussion should explain how the two products will be protected, what each source may establish, which lengths remain unresolved and what review is needed. A recommendation to use Module 14 should say why political analysis is needed and what the evidence can support. Review it with the other components; no separate set of analytical settings or extra Module 14 approval gate is required.

Phase 1 also previews which execution shapes look eligible. It stops before selecting the complete architecture. After reviewing the components and resolving consequential omissions, send CONFIRM CHAIN COMPONENTS. That permits Phase 2: the formal comparison of all three governed shapes and the complete proposed design.

Four routes, starting with ordinary work

Direct prompting remains sufficient for many small tasks. You provide the source, purpose and constraints, then check the result. It sits outside Prompt Maker's governed lifecycle. A request to extract the meeting date or improve the wording of a short internal note does not need to become a chain.

Governed one-prompt execution belongs inside that lifecycle. Understanding and design are approved first. The execution prompt then contains an embedded preflight: a check that the authority, source roles, reader, language and format are settled before drafting begins. A material conflict stops dependent work. This shape needs stable authority, a small bounded source packet, one product contract, no independent research or analytical-lens branch, and checks that one context can carry out reliably. It has no separate Prompt 00.

A compact workflow uses a small number of justified stages. Its first execution stage, Prompt 00, establishes the task authority and source map. Later stages remain blocked until that map passes its checks and you send APPROVE PROMPT 00. Compact work can then separate an evidence pass, drafting and review without creating a large research organization.

A full chain adds the stages or branches needed for substantial dependencies: separate evidence streams, context boundaries, an independent review, or a consequential final artifact. It retains the same Prompt 00 gate. Its extra stages must solve identifiable problems; page count alone is a poor guide to how much work is needed.

Consider three professional assignments:

Four routes, starting with ordinary work
Assignment Proportionate route and reason
A briefing paragraph explaining one supplied source for a defined reader Direct prompting usually suffices. If the organization requires this paragraph to use Prompt Maker's governed lifecycle, governed one-prompt may fit: the source and product are bounded, and the checks can stay together.
An options note requiring a small authorized search, one draft and a review return Compact is a plausible choice. The evidence must be checked before the recommendation is drafted, and review may send the draft back for repair. These are useful stage boundaries.
A comparative report from several long, changing source collections, followed by independent review and a formatted publication package A full chain may be justified. Evidence branches need comparable extraction, a checked merge, and review that is actually independent. Several simultaneous assistants without those controls would not solve the problem.

The route can change when the work changes. A supposedly small search may uncover contradictions that need separate investigation. Several long collections may already have a reliable, reconciled evidence pack, making some proposed branches redundant. Explain the stage boundaries through the actual problem they solve.

Compare approaches when the choice can change the work

The decision-diversity gate, Module 04, helps resist settling on the first familiar approach. It asks for materially different routes and a reasoned selection. For a policy options note, alternatives might be: compare each intervention in turn; organize the comparison around criteria such as reach, influence and feasibility; or begin with a binding constraint and eliminate options that cannot meet it. The first gives each option a coherent account, the second makes tradeoffs easier to compare, and the third helps when an option is genuinely infeasible. Select the structure that serves the decision and the available evidence. Three synonymous headings do not provide three useful alternatives.

The detailed rule uses two candidates for a narrow tactical decision, three by default, and four only for high-stakes architecture or source weighting. It is not a requirement to invent alternatives for factual extraction, quotation checking, confidentiality decisions or rendering an approved draft. There is one date in the note; three imaginative answers would make the work worse.

Compare the options against the task, evidence, reader, constraints and permitted operations. Calling a route “unusual” supplies no evidence that it will work. Ask for the relevant assumptions, trade-offs and unresolved risks, rather than private internal reasoning. Module 14 separately tests substantive political interpretations; Chapter 9 explains that distinction.

Carry Helen's two products into a current design

The following design applies the current method to Helen’s earlier assignment; it is not the historical HSC chain. Assume a small source packet that one evidence stage can review for both products. Keep drafting separate from review. For this example, neither an independent research branch nor an independent reviewer is required. Check these conditions during Phase 2 before choosing the route.

Under those conditions, compact work fits. A governed single prompt is poorly suited to the two different products and the requested separation of stages. A full chain would need a further reason, such as a genuinely independent research stream or review. Two products alone do not establish a need for thirteen stages.

The proposed compact design might begin with Prompt 00, then check the evidence, draft the oral opening and background briefing, and review and repair both. The final design specifies the real inputs, dependencies, source permissions, product limits, checks and permitted execution route. It stops for APPROVE CHAIN DESIGN.

That approval permits the creation of the operator artifact, the file containing the approved execution instructions. Governed one-prompt uses single_prompt_operator.html; compact and full work use prompt_chain_operator.html. These are method artifacts, not the speech or briefing. Design approval does not approve future claims or authorize sending documents to anyone.

For the compact example, execution starts with Prompt 00. Review its authority and source map against the original tasking and received sources. Once the required checks pass and you approve it with APPROVE PROMPT 00, dependent stages may proceed under their actual instructions. If review later finds that expanding the background briefing deleted an accepted point, the repair restores that point and checks the affected meaning and dependencies. It does not turn the briefing into a speech or restart unrelated sound work. Chapter 11 follows that repair in detail.

The same method in a manual chat and an agent environment

The Full Adapter supplies separate method files. Lean groups material for uploads and manual transfer between chats. Plugin packages the instructions for environments with supported skills and helpers. All three retain the applicable capabilities, checks and approvals. They differ in how the work is carried and whether a reusable knowledge collection is enabled by default.

In ordinary chat, the primary chat holds the task together. Follow the approved operator's actual stage instructions. Keep coherent work in that chat when it remains sufficient. If a fresh chat is justified by capacity, contamination, useful delegation or required independence, transfer the complete instructions, exact accepted inputs, source access and return destination. A fresh conversation cannot recover an omitted qualification merely because another chat knew it.

In an authorized agent environment, the primary agent may use permitted tools, assign bounded work, validate returns and continue authorized stages.
