An accurate document gets its claims right. A useful document helps someone do the job they came to it for. Good writing makes that help understandable in the intended form. These qualities overlap, but checking one does not check the others.

Helen, the speaker in this manual’s worked example, needs both a background briefing and opening remarks for a policy roundtable. A briefing could accurately summarise every article yet leave her unsure what point to raise. Adding a supported explanation of why the findings matter would make it more useful. Her speech could make exactly the right argument but bury it in long sentences that listeners cannot follow. That calls for a writing revision, not more research.

Review the claims against their sources; compare the result with the assignment; then read it as its audience will encounter it. For a speech, that includes reading it aloud. A factual correction, a missing argument and an overloaded sentence need different repairs.

Read in chapter 3: Identify the defect before correcting it

See also

  • source check / fact check
  • genre
  • review

Adapter

An Adapter is the form in which Prompt Maker’s instructions and working material reach the assistant. Full keeps the method in separate files; Lean groups material for uploads and manual handoffs; Plugin packages it for an environment that can use the supported skills and tools.

The forms differ in operation, not in how much truth or permission matters. Lean does not automatically enable a reusable knowledge collection, or wiki, but it still requires the applicable source checks and approvals. Use the Adapter actually supplied rather than assuming that a named file or skill exists in every chat.

Read in chapter 7: Choose and run the workflow

Affected set

The affected set is everything that may become wrong when you make a particular change. Correcting a survey total can change its percentage, the conclusion drawn from that percentage and a chart that repeats it. An unrelated introduction may need no change.

Follow the consequences of the edit and check those parts. A new speaking-time limit affects the length of the remarks without necessarily invalidating the background research. When you cannot tell where a changed fact has been reused, search more broadly rather than assuming the edited paragraph is the whole repair.

Agent

An agent is an AI assistant set up to pursue a task through a sequence of steps, using tools where available. It might search for reports, read them, compare findings and create a document, with the result of each operation informing its next step.

That ability makes the limits of the assignment important. “Research these public reports and return a draft; do not send it” permits a useful sequence without authorising publication. An agent can choose among available actions, but it cannot grant itself permission or make an unsuccessful operation succeed by describing it as complete.

Read in chapter 8: Delegate a question that can be checked

AGENTS.md

AGENTS.md is a file used to give Codex instructions that should apply across tasks in a particular scope. It might specify a team’s writing conventions or the checks required before changing project files. Codex has rules for discovering and combining global and project guidance; a file with this name in an unrelated folder does not automatically govern everything.

These are working instructions, not evidence for a report’s factual claims. A rule to use a certain citation style still leaves the sources to be read and checked. Other chat environments may handle project instructions differently.

Read in chapter 8: What a skill or plugin contributes

AI assistant

An AI assistant is the system you work with, including the application, the model, the material supplied for the task and any available tools. The model generates responses; the application provides the interface and manages capabilities; tools can perform operations such as reading a file or saving a document.

These parts can succeed or fail separately. The assistant may draft a good paragraph while lacking the tool needed to create the requested PDF. Look for the result of the relevant operation, not just a sentence saying that it happened. Producing a recommendation does not make it an approved decision.

Read in chapter 2: The assistant is more than the model

See also

  • model
  • context
  • generation

Analysis / interpretation

Analysis explains what information means for a question. Interpretation offers a reasoned account of its significance. Both go beyond repeating a source, but their conclusions still have to fit the evidence.

Suppose a staff survey reports that many respondents avoid a training course because its sessions clash with their shifts. A summary repeats that finding. An analysis explains that scheduling may be limiting access, so revising the timetable is worth considering before commissioning new course content. It must also retain the survey’s limits: respondents are not necessarily representative of all staff, and the survey does not prove that a timetable change would raise attendance.

Ask for the connection between the finding and the proposed action, together with any reason that connection might not hold. This produces useful interpretation without pretending that the source has already tested the recommendation.

Read in chapter 9: Turn evidence into analysis

See also

  • inference
  • synthesis

App

An app is the software you use to work with AI, such as ChatGPT or a desktop interface for Codex. It provides the interface, controls and available tools. The model is the trained system that generates responses within that application.

Read in chapter 1: Before you start

See also

  • model
  • tool

Approval receipt

An approval receipt records exactly what someone approved and for which next step. In Prompt Maker, it can identify the version of a task-understanding brief approved for designing the workflow.

Keep the receipt with that version. A later draft that changes the required products cannot borrow the earlier approval without the relevant review. The receipt establishes a decision; it does not prove that every factual statement in the approved document is correct.

See also

  • external action
  • operator artifact
  • prompt

Argument line / framing

An argument line is the central idea that connects a document’s evidence and conclusions. Framing is the perspective used to organise the question. A report on delayed training could be framed around staff motivation, access to sessions or management capacity. Each directs attention to different evidence.

Choose a frame that helps answer the assignment rather than one that merely sounds persuasive. If the evidence points to shift conflicts, an argument about access is better supported than a confident claim that staff lack motivation. State the connection clearly enough for the reader to challenge it.

Read in chapter 9: Compare genuinely different approaches

Artifact

An artifact is a concrete output: a document, spreadsheet, image or other produced item. For a file task, the artifact is the actual file with its contents, not the assistant’s description of what it intends to create. Open the delivered version when checking whether the requested work exists and is usable.

Read in chapter 3: An answer can finish before the task is finished

See also

  • file path

Assumption

An assumption is something you provisionally treat as true so that work can proceed, although it has not been established. Its limits should be clear.

For example, you could outline remarks for a provisional ten-minute slot while keeping them easy to shorten. That is different from telling the speaker that ten minutes has been confirmed. Explain the basis for the assumption and what would change if it proved wrong. Do not assume approval, a policy commitment or a research finding merely because doing so would make drafting easier.

Attribution

Attribution tells the reader whose statement, finding or interpretation you are reporting. “The evaluation’s authors report higher attendance” identifies an account; “the ministry has adopted this approach” attributes an institutional decision and needs different support.

Name the relevant author or institution, and retain the date or scope when it affects the meaning. Attribution does not excuse a distorted paraphrase: the attributed source must actually say what your sentence claims.

Read in chapter 4: Give each source a permitted role

Authority

Authority concerns who can decide something, and what a source can establish for the purpose at hand. A commissioner can set the requested length of a briefing. An agenda can establish the planned meeting time. A research article can support its authors’ findings. None of these automatically answers the others’ questions.

When sources conflict, ask which one has authority over this particular requirement or claim. A new assistant summary cannot override the original request, and an external analyst’s recommendation cannot become a ministry commitment without the appropriate decision.

Read in chapter 4: Give each source a permitted role

Authorization / permission

Authorisation is permission to perform a particular action on particular material. Reading, editing and sending a document are separate actions, even when one tool can do all three.

Permission to consult an internal note for a briefing does not by itself allow copying it into a public search query or sending it to an outside service. Keep the task’s boundaries explicit, and obtain the required permission before taking an action outside them.

Read in chapter 4: Reading and sharing are different actions

Bibliography

A bibliography identifies the works used in a document, usually with details such as author, title and date. It lets a reader find the sources, but may not show which passage supports each claim. Where the chosen citation system requires it, pair bibliography entries with matching references in the text. A well-formatted source list is useful navigation, not a substitute for checking the claims.

Read in chapter 10: Choose how the reader sees the evidence

See also

  • citation
  • footnote
  • hyperlink citation

Branch / merge

A branch is a separately handled part of a larger task. A merge brings the returned work together and resolves differences before it becomes one answer.

For example, two helpers might extract findings from different country reports. One report covers a calendar year and the other only six months. The merge must preserve that distinction; pasting the summaries together and comparing their totals would be misleading. Check each return, reconcile definitions and limits, and decide what the combined evidence actually supports.

Read in chapter 8: Delegate a question that can be checked

Browsing

Browsing means using web tools to find and read online material. A search result is a route to a source; opening and inspecting the relevant page is another step. Searching today can still lead to an old report, and a freshly opened page can still be wrong. Check the publication’s date, purpose and actual supporting passage.

Read in chapter 8: Work with sources, tools, skills and helpers

Canonical / controlling version

The controlling, or canonical, version is the version that governs the current work. It is not necessarily the file with the newest timestamp or the word “final” in its name.

A team may have approved version 2 while version 3 remains an experiment. Identify the approved version and keep proposed changes separate until they have passed the required review. Otherwise a well-intentioned edit can silently replace an agreed decision.

Read in chapter 5: Keep the current decision identifiable

Capability, availability and authorization

Three questions determine whether an assistant can properly carry out an operation. Capability: can the system do this kind of work? Availability: are the necessary tools and sources usable in this session? Authorisation: is this particular action permitted?

A model may be good at comparing reports while one report is inaccessible. It may produce the comparison successfully while having no permission to email it. Product documentation can describe a capability without establishing either access in your account or permission for your task.

Read in chapter 5: Match reasoning to the difficulty

See also

  • evidence
  • tool

Causation versus association

An association means two things vary together. A causal claim says that changing one produces a change in the other. The second claim needs more than a pattern or a sequence of events.

Attendance might rise after a course moves online, but the same period might also bring compulsory participation or a larger staff group. Those changes could explain the increase. Report the observed rise accurately; before attributing it to the online format, look for evidence that addresses the alternatives. A confident “therefore” does not supply that evidence.

Chain / prompt chain

A prompt chain organises work across several requests or stages, sometimes with parallel branches. One stage returns material another needs: checked findings can feed a draft, and review findings can feed a repair.

Use a chain when these boundaries solve a real problem, such as comparing several long reports without losing their definitions. A short paragraph based on one clear passage may need only a direct request and a source check. More stages create more handoffs to manage; they are not evidence of better reasoning.

Read in chapter 7: Choose and run the workflow

Changed brief

A brief is the assignment. A changed brief alters what is being asked for: perhaps a different audience, a shorter contribution or a new purpose.

A two-page background note and a later one-page contribution should be judged against their respective requests. The later text being shorter does not prove that the first exceeded its original limit. In the manual’s International Criminal Court briefing episode, the requested use and length evolved alongside collaborative editing. Those changes matter when interpreting differences between drafts.

Read in chapter 9: Why the ICC episode matters

Chat / conversation / thread

A chat, conversation or thread is an exchange of messages and its recorded history. It is a place to develop an assignment, supply sources and correct decisions. The visible history is not necessarily identical to all the material the model receives for every response. Make a consequential update explicit—for example, which outline replaces the old one—rather than relying on the assistant to infer the current decision from a long exchange.

Read in chapter 1: Before you start

ChatGPT

ChatGPT is OpenAI’s application for working with an AI assistant through conversations and supported tools. A simple task might involve pasting a passage and asking for a summary; a larger one might involve project sources, research and document creation. The available tools, models and controls depend on the product and account. Use the capabilities actually present rather than assuming that a feature described elsewhere is enabled in your session.

Read in chapter 1: Before you start

See also

  • Codex
  • evidence
  • tool

ChatGPT Work

ChatGPT Work is a mode for pursuing larger tasks and deliverables where it is available. It uses the sources, tools and permissions provided by its environment. A document task still needs the actual sources and a result you can inspect; the mode’s name does not establish access in every account. It is an application feature, not a Prompt Maker module.

Read in chapter 5: Choose the environment for the actual work

See also

  • ChatGPT
  • Codex
  • desktop app / local project

Checkpoint

A checkpoint records where the work actually stands so that it can be resumed. It identifies the current version, decisions already made, remaining gaps and next permitted action.

“Draft saved; PDF not yet exported or inspected; next step is export and page review” is more useful than “mostly done.” It preserves completed work while making the unfinished part visible. A checkpoint records approval only when that approval has actually occurred.

Read in chapter 5: Keep the current decision identifiable

Citation

A citation is a reference connecting a claim to its source. It may appear as a hyperlink, an in-text reference or a note, depending on the document’s requirements. A precise page or section reference makes the evidence easier to inspect.

The source must support the claim beside it. A real article announcing a proposed programme does not establish that the programme was implemented successfully. Follow the citation and compare the wording, including its dates, limits and certainty.

Read in chapter 10: Choose how the reader sees the evidence

See also

  • evidence
  • YAML
  • bibliography

Claim / proposition

A claim is something a statement asserts. “The consultation changed the policy” asserts an outcome; “the consultation was proposed” asserts an intention at an earlier stage. These are different claims and require different evidence. Before checking a sentence, identify exactly what it says happened, who was involved and how certain it sounds.

Read in chapter 3: False and unverified are different findings

See also

  • evidence

Claim support / entailment

Claim support asks whether the evidence warrants the statement you have written. Entailment is a stricter logical term: whether a conclusion follows from its premises. In source checking, the practical question is whether the wording goes beyond what the source establishes.

A note saying “the board will consider the proposal next month” does not support “the board approved the proposal.” Both mention the same board and proposal, but differ in action, time and status. Matching keywords or attaching the note as a citation does not repair the difference.

Read in chapter 4: Give each source a permitted role

Classification / transformation

Classification assigns items to categories, such as labelling meeting statements “decision” or “proposal.” Transformation changes their form, such as turning a note into a table or translating it into another language.

Specify the rule and what meaning must stay unchanged. Reformatting a proposal under an “Agreed actions” heading changes its status, even though most of the original words remain. Neither task is permission to fill empty fields with invented facts.

Read in chapter 4: What an example adds

Codex

Codex is OpenAI’s agent environment for working on tasks with accessible files, instructions and tools. It is used extensively for code, but available file and document tools can also support research, editing and professional documents.

The relevant question is what the particular environment can read and do. A reference to a folder on your computer does not give a remote session access to it. Establish the working area and permitted operations before relying on a file-based result.

Read in chapter 1: Before you start

See also

  • ChatGPT
  • tool
  • desktop app / local project

Compact workflow

A compact workflow is a Prompt Maker task divided into a few justified stages rather than a large chain. It can keep evidence review, drafting and a return for corrections separate when those steps have different inputs and checks.

Compact work still begins execution with Prompt 00, the task-authority and source-map stage. Dependent stages wait for its checks and APPROVE PROMPT 00. “Compact” means fewer necessary boundaries, not skipped approvals or weaker evidence. Use the approved design to determine the actual stages.

Read in chapter 7: Four routes, starting with ordinary work

See also

  • evidence
  • execution shape
  • fresh chat

Compaction

Compaction reduces the amount of earlier conversation carried forward so a long interaction can continue with less context. A system may use a summary or a compact representation designed for the model.

Reduced size is useful, but it is not a promise that every detail remains available exactly as written. Keep important decisions and references to original sources in explicit records. If a later answer loses an exception from a report, return to that passage rather than treating the compacted account as the source itself.

Read in chapter 5: Several different limits can look like forgetting

Component

In Prompt Maker’s chain design, a component is a control or piece of work being considered for inclusion. Research might be needed because a current source is missing; a separate review might be needed because the result will be published. Reviewing components settles what needs to be included before the complete workflow is designed. Confirming them is not yet approval to execute the finished design.

Read in chapter 7: First choose the controls; then design the stages

Confidence

Confidence is the degree of certainty attached to a claim. It is useful only when you can relate it to the evidence. An assistant’s “95% confident” is not, by itself, a measured probability that the statement is true.

A more useful assessment names the support and the gap: “The agenda confirms the meeting date, but the speaker’s individual time slot is not confirmed.” That tells you what can be used and what still needs checking, without making every sentence sound doubtful.

Read in chapter 3: Keep checking proportionate and specific

See also

  • evidence

Confidentiality / necessary disclosure

Confidentiality concerns who may receive information and for what purpose. Necessary disclosure means supplying only the information the authorised task requires.

An internal draft can be appropriate input in an approved system while remaining inappropriate for a public search query. A tool connection or an advanced model does not change that boundary. Consider the material, the service receiving it and the audience of the finished product separately.

Read in chapter 4: Reading and sharing are different actions

Connector

A connector is a route between the AI application and an external service, such as a document store. It exposes particular operations under particular permissions. A connector that can search and read files may not be able to edit them. A connected account also does not imply access to every file in that account. Check the operation and the material needed for the task.

Read in chapter 8: What a skill or plugin contributes

See also

  • MCP
  • plugin
  • skill

Contaminated context

Context is contaminated when irrelevant, obsolete or conflicting material influences work that it should not govern. An old instruction to write a speech might remain beside a newer request for a background note, leaving the assistant to mix the two.

Resolve the conflict explicitly: identify the current product and which instruction it replaces. A long conversation is not automatically contaminated, and a new conversation will not help if you copy the same unresolved conflict into it.

Read in chapter 5: Several different limits can look like forgetting

Context

Context is the material available to the model while it produces the current response. It can include your request, applicable instructions, earlier messages, source passages, tool results and text already generated. It is not the same as everything stored in your account or visible in a project folder.

Imagine asking for a comparison of three reports. The model may know a great deal about the subject in general, but it still needs the relevant contents of those particular reports. A filename supplies an identity, not the findings inside it. The application may retrieve selected passages rather than place every report into the input at once.

Supply the current assignment and make the relevant sources accessible. When the answer misses a correction or misstates a report, establish what material was actually available and then check how it was used. Missing input and misinterpreted input are different problems.

Read in chapter 2: The assistant is more than the model

See also

  • model
  • generation
  • token

Context assembly

Context assembly is the application’s work of putting together the input for a response. It may combine instructions, selected conversation history and material retrieved from files or tools. A project containing ten reports might contribute only the passages found for the current question.

This explains why storing a document and using its contents are separate events. When complete coverage matters, ask which versions and ranges were examined. The model’s general knowledge cannot fill in missing facts from a private project.

Read in chapter 5: Several different limits can look like forgetting

Context engineering

Context engineering means arranging the information an assistant needs for the next piece of work. It includes selecting sources, retaining current decisions and keeping obsolete drafts from competing with the accepted version. Prompt wording is part of this, but adding more words is not the objective.

For a report revision, a useful input might be the accepted draft, the new evidence and a precise change request. Sending every past draft without saying which one governs can make the job harder rather than better informed.

See also

  • prompt engineering
  • tool

Context rot

“Context rot” is an informal name for reduced reliability in some long or noisy AI interactions. The assistant may miss a correction, revive an abandoned outline or confuse the facts in two drafts, even when the relevant material has not literally been cut off. It is not a fixed expiry time or a universal loss of accuracy per message.

A common practical problem is competition between versions. After many revisions, a long old draft may sit beside a short but important instruction changing its purpose. The next answer follows the old pattern. That observation tells you what failed; it does not prove which internal mechanism caused it.

Start with the smallest useful repair: restate the current decision, identify the accepted draft and remove ambiguity about what must change. Check the next result. A fresh chat can help when accumulated material is genuinely getting in the way, but it needs a handoff containing the actual task, sources, accepted decisions and unresolved points. Copying the entire confused history merely moves the problem.

Read in chapter 5: Several different limits can look like forgetting

See also

  • context
  • handoff
  • fresh chat

Context window

The context window is the finite amount of information a model can handle for a response, measured in tokens—the pieces used to represent text. The model also has limits on how much output it can produce. These limits are related, but an advertised context capacity is not a promise of an answer that long.

A large collection may need selective retrieval or compaction rather than being inserted in full. Even when everything could fit, the application must actually supply the relevant material, and the model must use it correctly. More capacity does not establish either condition. Check whether a returned passage or answer was cut off instead of assuming that a large window guarantees complete reading.

Read in chapter 5: Several different limits can look like forgetting

See also

  • retrieval
  • token

Controlled comparison / causal attribution limits

A controlled comparison tries to distinguish the effect of one change from other influences. To test whether a prompt improves a briefing, you would need to keep relevant conditions comparable: the assignment, source packet and evaluation criteria, for example.

Two documents are not such a test when the brief changed, new sources arrived and colleagues edited the later draft. You can describe the differences and consider possible explanations, but cannot assign all improvement to a particular model or rule. This is why the manual treats its historical briefing episodes as learning examples, not model rankings.

Read in chapter 9: Why the ICC episode matters

Counterargument / strongest objection

A counterargument is a reason your interpretation or recommendation might not hold. The strongest useful objection is one that could change the conclusion, not a generic sentence saying that the issue is complicated.

A report might recommend an online consultation because it reached many respondents. A serious objection is that the same recruitment channels may exclude people without reliable internet access. That could change both the recommended method and the claims made about whose views it represents. Address the objection with evidence, a narrower conclusion or a different choice.

Currentness / knowledge freshness

Information is current when its date and scope are suitable for the decision being made. A report opened today may describe last year’s policy, and a model’s general knowledge may omit a recent change. Check the date of the underlying information, not just the date on which it was retrieved. For changeable matters such as product features or office-holders, consult appropriate current sources.

Read in chapter 12: Keep a lesson when it will help another task

D–G

Decision diversity

Decision diversity means considering approaches that differ in a consequential way before choosing one. An options note might examine each option in turn, compare options against shared criteria, or begin with a constraint that rules some out. These structures help the reader think differently; three introductions with different adjectives do not.

Compare the alternatives against the assignment, evidence and practical limits. Prompt Maker’s Module 04 uses two candidates for a narrow tactical choice, three by default and four only for high-stakes architecture or source-weighting decisions. This is not a requirement to invent alternatives to an exact date, a quotation or a settled fact. Module 14’s comparison of political interpretations is a separate control.

See also

  • evidence

Demonstration / example prompting

An example can show an assistant what a written instruction leaves vague. A previous briefing might demonstrate a direct opening, moderate paragraph length and unobtrusive citations.

Specify which features should transfer. “Follow the sample’s structure and level of explanation; use the new reports for facts” is different from asking for a close adaptation of its content. Without that distinction, a useful style example can carry old figures, conclusions or commitments into the new work.

Read in chapter 4: What an example adds

See also

  • governed one prompt
  • zero-shot / one-shot / few-shot

Dependencies

A dependency is a relationship in which one part of the work relies on another. A recommendation may depend on a calculation, which depends on a source figure. Correcting the figure means checking the calculation and recommendation too. Follow those relationships when reviewing a change; neither rewriting everything nor inspecting only the edited sentence is automatically sufficient.

Read in chapter 7: Choose and run the workflow

Desktop app / local project

A desktop app is software running on your computer. A local project is a selected working area, usually connected to one or more folders. Installing an app does not give every task unrestricted access to your files. Establish which folder the session can actually read or change. A path on your computer may mean nothing to a remote environment.

Read in chapter 5: Choose the environment for the actual work

See also

  • ChatGPT
  • Codex
  • evidence

Deterministic extraction

Deterministic extraction uses a fixed rule to obtain the same result from the same input—for example, copying the text between two known headings with a program. It differs from an open-ended request to interpret the passage.

A language model being asked to extract something does not automatically make the process deterministic. Exact wording, dates and commands still need comparison with the original. Even a perfectly repeatable extraction can select the wrong passage if its rule is wrong.

See also

  • evidence

Discovery lead

A discovery lead helps you find evidence. It might be a search snippet, a colleague’s suggestion or a newsletter linking to a research article. Follow it to the underlying source before relying on the finding. A newsletter’s mention can explain why you looked at an article; it does not replace reading it or turn the author’s view into your institution’s position.

Read in chapter 8: Work with sources, tools, skills and helpers

Evidence

Evidence is material that supports or challenges a particular claim. Its value depends on the question. A dated agenda is evidence of the planned event; an attendance record is evidence about who came. Neither, by itself, proves what effect the event had.

Compare the exact assertion with what the material establishes. “The programme was proposed,” “it began” and “it improved outcomes” require different support. Collecting several sources about the topic does not bridge those gaps. The relationship between the claim and the evidence matters more than the number of links.

Read in chapter 3: False and unverified are different findings

See also

  • citation
  • independent review
  • prompt

Execution shape

Execution shape is Prompt Maker’s term for how an approved task is organised during execution. Governed one-prompt work keeps a small task and its checks together. A compact workflow separates a few necessary stages. A full chain adds stages or branches for more substantial evidence, handoff or review needs.

The choice follows the work, not just the length of the answer. A short recommendation can require extensive research; a longer summary of one stable document may be straightforward. Formal comparison of the three shapes happens after component confirmation in chain design.

Read in chapter 7: Choose and run the workflow

See also

  • evidence
  • compact workflow
  • fresh chat

External action

An external action changes something beyond the current drafting work, such as sending an email, publishing a page or updating a shared record. Preparing the text and carrying out the action are different steps. Check both permission and the result in the relevant system. A draft message is not a sent message, and a sent document is not necessarily accepted by its recipient.

Read in chapter 3: Match the check to the claim

See also

  • approval receipt
  • operator artifact
  • prompt

Extractive summary / quote listing

An extractive summary selects or shortens source passages. A quote list collects their exact wording. Both can be useful research records, but may leave the reader to work out the relationship between findings.

A note that says “one report describes low attendance; another describes shift conflicts” still needs to explain why those findings belong together. A briefing might examine whether scheduling limits access, while making clear that the reports do not establish the cause. Use the extracts as support for the answer the reader needs, rather than assuming that a source-by-source list is always the safest finished product.

Read in chapter 9: Grounded composition: the freedom you actually need

False completion

False completion means reporting that work is finished when the required result or check has not been established. “The PDF is ready” is false completion if only a Word draft exists. “All sources checked” is unsupported if only a file listing was examined.

Separate the claims in the closing message. Does the file exist? Is it the requested version? Were its pages inspected? Was it sent, and was sending authorised? Preserve work that is genuinely complete and ask for the specific missing operation. A more confident status sentence cannot perform it.

Read in chapter 3: An answer can finish before the task is finished

See also

  • hallucination to completion / completion pressure

File path

A file path is an address for a file in a particular environment, such as reports/briefing.docx. It tells you where to look, not whether the file exists, opens correctly or is accessible from another computer. A path written in a chat is not evidence that the assistant saved anything there.

Read in chapter 3: An answer can finish before the task is finished

See also

  • artifact

Footnote

A footnote is a note linked to a point in the main text and usually placed at the bottom of the page. It can supply a source or supporting detail without putting all of it in the sentence. Follow the citation format agreed for the document. In a short briefing, selective notes may help; in spoken remarks, the evidence is usually kept in the supporting record. Check that notes remain readable in the actual exported document.

Read in chapter 10: Choose how the reader sees the evidence

See also

  • bibliography
  • citation
  • hyperlink citation

Freeze

To freeze an understanding in Prompt Maker is to turn the discussion into a fixed candidate that can be reviewed. FINALIZE TASK UNDERSTANDING produces that candidate; it does not approve it. The candidate remains awaiting_operator_approval until the separate approval. It can still be corrected and replaced before that decision.

Read in chapter 6: The six Understand states, as a conversation

Fresh chat

A fresh chat starts a new conversation, but not necessarily an empty or isolated context. The application may still supply project instructions, files or memory. It can reduce distracting conversation history, but you should explicitly supply the decisions and sources the next task needs. For independent review, check what information the reviewer can access; opening a new chat alone is not enough.

For a briefing revision, carry the current assignment, accepted draft, relevant sources, requested change and unresolved decisions into the new chat. “Continue the work from earlier” is not enough when that earlier work is unavailable. Use a new chat for a reason—capacity, conflicting context, a bounded separate task or required review independence—not as an automatic response to every mistake.

Read in chapter 5: Keep the current decision identifiable

See also

  • evidence
  • compact workflow
  • execution shape

Full chain

A full chain is a Prompt Maker workflow with the stages or branches required for substantial dependencies. Several long source collections may need separate extraction, reconciliation and independent review before publication.

Its execution still starts with Prompt 00 and the required approval of the task-authority and source map. Each extra stage should have a clear purpose, adequate inputs and a checkable return. Two products do not automatically require a full chain, and many assistants producing text do not automatically produce a sound combined result.

Read in chapter 7: Four routes, starting with ordinary work

See also

  • evidence
  • governed one prompt
  • independent review

Gate / stop gate

A gate is a condition that must be met before dependent work can continue. It may require a missing source, a passed check or a specific human approval. The point is to prevent work from relying on something unresolved.

A gate should identify what is blocking progress and what would resolve it. It is not a reason to ask for approval of every ordinary sentence. In-scope drafting and repairs can continue under valid existing authority; a consequential new decision returns to its actual decision point.

Read in chapter 6: The six Understand states, as a conversation

Generation

Generation is the production of an output from the model’s current input. In a simplified account of text generation, the model estimates possible next pieces of text, one is selected, and the growing sequence becomes part of the input for the next step.

This can produce fluent, connected prose without independently checking every factual claim. Once a paragraph introduces an unsupported success story, later sentences may elaborate its supposed benefits. Their consistency does not verify the starting claim. Check generated claims against evidence rather than treating a coherent story as confirmation.

Read in chapter 2: How a response grows

See also

  • context
  • model
  • instructions

Genre

Genre is the kind of writing that serves a particular use. A speech has to be understood as listeners hear it; a background briefing can include evidence and qualifications that a reader revisits; an options note helps someone compare choices.

Changing headings does not change the genre on its own. Select and order the material for the intended use. The same evidence can support both a briefing and a speech without requiring the speech to read the briefing aloud.

Read in chapter 4: Begin with the reader's use

See also

  • evidence

Governed one prompt

Governed one-prompt execution is Prompt Maker’s smallest governed execution shape. Task understanding and design are approved first. One execution prompt then contains the necessary work and an embedded preflight: it checks authority, source roles, reader and product requirements before drafting.

It fits a stable, bounded source packet and one product whose checks can be handled reliably together, without an independent research or analytical branch. A material conflict stops the dependent work. There is no separate Prompt 00 in this shape.

This is not the same as an ordinary direct request outside the lifecycle. Nor is it “one-shot prompting,” which counts the examples supplied in a request rather than the organisation of the task.

Read in chapter 7: Four routes, starting with ordinary work

See also

  • evidence
  • full chain
  • zero-shot / one-shot / few-shot

Grounding

Grounding keeps factual statements tied to identifiable evidence. The relevant material must be available, understood correctly and strong enough to support the wording.

Grounded writing can still explain, compare and draw qualified conclusions. “Use only the supplied reports” need not mean “write only quotations.” It means that new prose cannot quietly introduce an unsupported event, causal claim or institutional commitment. Retain the source trail so the important connections can be checked.

Read in chapter 9: Grounded composition: the freedom you actually need

H–L

Hallucination

A hallucination is plausible AI-generated content that is false. A fabricated quotation or a citation to a nonexistent report are clear examples. A different problem is a claim that has not been verified: it may be true, but you do not yet have grounds to rely on it. Absence from one source does not by itself prove falsity.

A model generates from learned patterns and the input available to it; producing a likely continuation is not the same as checking a claim against reality. Missing knowledge, missing or misused source material and training incentives to guess can contribute to errors. None of those general explanations proves why a particular answer went wrong.

Suppose a source says a consultation is planned, while a draft says it has already improved policy. The draft misrepresents what that source establishes. Check for evidence of implementation and results; until then, restore the supported status instead of adding confidence. Correct false claims, and verify, qualify or omit unsupported ones as the assignment requires. An omission, a failed file operation or awkward writing needs attention too, but is not automatically a hallucination.

Read in chapter 3: False and unverified are different findings

See also

  • claim support / entailment
  • source check / fact check
  • false completion

Hallucination to completion / completion pressure

“Hallucination to completion” and “completion pressure” are informal labels for an assistant claiming to have finished work without the required evidence. They describe a pattern, not an official OpenAI status or proof of deliberate deception.

For example, an assistant may say “all files read” after listing an archive, or “the export looks good” after saving a file without opening it. Ask which operation actually ran, what it returned and what remains unchecked. Repair the missing step rather than accepting a polished closing message.

Read in chapter 3: An answer can finish before the task is finished

See also

  • false completion

Handoff

A handoff gives another person, chat or helper enough to continue the work correctly. It carries the purpose as well as the files: the current assignment, accepted inputs, relevant evidence, constraints, unresolved points, required return and person responsible for checking it.

A helper asked to extract a report needs to know which question the report must inform. Otherwise it can produce an accurate but irrelevant summary. Include exact versions and accessible source references; an assurance that another chat read them does not supply their contents.

Read in chapter 5: Keep the current decision identifiable

See also

  • evidence

Hard budget

A hard budget is a binding limit, such as two pages, 150 words or a confirmed five-minute speaking slot. Say what the limit includes: two pages of main text is different from two pages including notes and annexes.

Meeting it requires selection, not merely smaller type. Decide what is essential and what can be cut first. A shared opening block on an agenda is not automatically the individual speaker’s time allowance; confirm that distinction before treating an estimate as a hard limit.

Read in chapter 4: Begin with the reader's use

Hash

A hash is a computed fingerprint of content. It helps identify whether the file being checked is the same one that was reviewed earlier. Changing the content normally changes its hash.

This is useful when an approval must apply to a specific proposal rather than to whatever a later file happens to contain. A matching fingerprint is evidence about identity, not proof that the contents are accurate, approved or successfully delivered.

Hidden reasoning / chain-of-thought

Chain-of-thought can refer to intermediate reasoning steps; a model’s private internal reasoning is not the same as the explanation it gives you. You do not need a transcript of that private process to evaluate an answer.

Ask instead for the relevant evidence, assumptions, connection to the conclusion and a serious objection. For example, an explanation of why two survey percentages cannot be combined should identify their different populations and periods. Those reasons are checkable; a lengthy account of supposed internal thoughts is not a substitute.

Human approval

Human approval is a person’s explicit acceptance of a particular decision or version for a stated purpose. In Prompt Maker, APPROVE TASK UNDERSTANDING approves the reviewed brief for chain design. It does not approve an unwritten final document or authorise sending it.

Keep the decision tied to what was reviewed. Silence, a request for corrections or an encouraging comment is not automatically the approval required by a gate.

Read in chapter 6: The six Understand states, as a conversation

See also

  • independent review
  • citation
  • evidence

Hyperlink citation

A hyperlink citation places a source reference in clickable text, usually a meaningful phrase or the source’s title. It lets a reader inspect support without inserting a full bibliographic entry into the sentence. Use links selectively and point to the relevant original. “Read the evaluation’s findings” tells a reader more than repeated “click here” links. The linked passage still needs to support the claim.

Read in chapter 10: Choose how the reader sees the evidence

See also

  • bibliography
  • citation
  • footnote

Immediate recipient / ultimate audience

The immediate recipient is the person who receives your work first. The ultimate audience is who will eventually read or hear it. Their needs can differ.

A colleague preparing remarks may need full sentences, background notes and room to edit; the audience hearing the final speech needs a clear spoken argument. Specify both uses when commissioning the work. A contribution for someone else to integrate should not automatically be written as a finished publication in that person’s name.

Read in chapter 10: One evidence base, two different uses

See also

  • reader baseline

Independent review

Independent review gives work scrutiny sufficiently separate from its production to challenge the assumptions behind it. The reviewer needs the actual candidate, relevant original sources and criteria, not just the producer’s summary of why it is correct.

A new chat or a different model name does not create independence by itself. A reviewer who receives only the same flawed digest may repeat the same omission. Give the reviewer room to disagree and return specific findings for repair. Several assistants agreeing is not stronger than the evidence they all relied on.

Read in chapter 8: Delegate a question that can be checked

See also

  • evidence
  • full chain
  • fresh chat

Inference

An inference is a conclusion drawn from premises rather than simply repeated from a source. If one note says a training session clashes with the late shift and another records low attendance among late-shift staff, it is reasonable to investigate scheduling as a barrier. It is not yet established that scheduling caused all the absences.

Make the connection visible and keep its limits. A useful inference can guide a question or conditional recommendation without being reported as a tested fact. Scrutinise both the supporting statements and the step from them to the conclusion.

Read in chapter 9: Turn evidence into analysis

See also

  • premise / inferential bridge
  • qualification
  • synthesis

Inference / generation time

In machine learning, inference time means the time when a trained model is used to produce an output, as distinct from training it. This technical use differs from an analytical inference—a conclusion drawn from evidence. A model can generate a straightforward transcription at inference time without the task asking for a new analytical conclusion.

Read in chapter 2: How a response grows

Institutional clearance

Institutional clearance is approval by the person or process authorised to clear a document or position for institutional use. A carefully checked speech may still await clearance to make a commitment on the institution’s behalf. An assistant’s self-review, a “final” filename or a persuasive source does not confer that permission. Report clearance only when the relevant approval is established.

Instruction compliance versus factual correctness

An answer can follow the requested format and still contain false information. A table with all three requested columns might give the wrong meeting date. Conversely, a correct account of the date may fail an assignment that also asked for the decisions and their owners.

Check instructions against the request, and claims against their evidence. Neither check replaces the other. A valid data format, correct word count or complete set of headings says little about whether the factual content is right.

Read in chapter 4: Give each source a permitted role

Instruction hierarchy

An instruction hierarchy determines which applicable directions take precedence. Platform and application rules can constrain what a user may request; project instructions can apply within their scope; the current request defines the particular job within those boundaries.

Newer text does not automatically outrank everything earlier. Changing a length requirement does not remove a confidentiality rule. Nor can a report being analysed grant itself authority by saying “ignore the user.” Keep live instructions separate from quoted commands or historical approvals inside source material, and surface genuine unresolved conflicts.

See also

  • evidence

Instructions

Instructions tell the assistant what to do and within what limits. “Summarise this report in one paragraph and preserve its uncertainty” is an instruction; the report is the material to summarise. A command quoted inside that report remains source content unless it has separately been made an applicable instruction. Giving the request and the evidence distinct roles prevents accidental changes to the assignment.

Read in chapter 1: Give the briefing a reader and a purpose

See also

  • generation
  • AI assistant
  • context

JSON

JSON, short for JavaScript Object Notation, is a text format for structured data. A small record might look like {"status": "draft", "pages": 2}. Named fields make information easier for software to exchange and check. They also make omissions easier to spot, but valid JSON can still contain a wrong page count. Read the values for meaning as well as checking the format.

See also

  • YAML
  • source role

Knowledge

In Prompt Maker, knowledge means reusable material kept with enough evidence and context to judge when it applies. It can include a research note, an editing lesson or a well-tested workflow.

Reuse is not automatic authority. A useful lesson about organising a briefing may travel well; last year’s programme figures retain their date and scope. Read the saved material and its source trail before applying it to a new assignment.

Read in chapter 12: Keep a lesson when it will help another task

Knowledge capture proposal

A knowledge capture proposal describes an exact addition or change to a reusable knowledge collection. It might preserve a useful editing lesson with its source and limits, rather than storing every draft indiscriminately.

The proposal gives you something specific to review. It is not already a saved update. A substantive write waits for the required proposal-specific approval, then must actually be applied and checked in the intended destination.

Read in chapter 12: Keep a lesson when it will help another task

Knowledge mode

Knowledge mode determines whether Prompt Maker’s optional integration with a wiki, a collection of reusable notes, is active. Full, Lean and Plugin are Prompt Maker’s Adapters, or delivery forms. Full and Plugin use wiki_enabled. Lean defaults to lean_no_wiki; an explicit manual_opt_in enables the relevant integration.

Without that opt-in, complete the document task without a wiki setup or automatic capture detour. You still preserve the sources needed to check the work. Supplying an old note as evidence, or requesting a standalone exported note, does not silently authorise continuing updates to a collection.

Read in chapter 12: Keep a lesson when it will help another task

See also

  • Adapter
  • Wiki

Large language model / LLM

A large language model, or LLM, is a trained system that generates language from patterns learned across substantial amounts of data. Training adjusts numerical settings inside the model. During use, those settings and the current input shape the response.

The model is not normally retrieving a complete stored answer for each request. It can work with a new report supplied in a conversation without being retrained on that report. This makes it useful for unfamiliar documents, but fluent writing is not evidence that it understood every passage or got every claim right. Supply the actual task material and check the result.

Read in chapter 2: What training changes

See also

  • model
  • model weights / parameters
  • training (model training)

Latency / resource trade-off

Latency is the time you wait for a response or operation. Resource trade-offs include the computation, tool work and human effort needed to reach a usable result.

A fast draft that takes three repair rounds may cost more time overall than a careful first pass. Extra helpers can reduce waiting on independent work but add checking and coordination. Choose enough effort for the difficulty and consequences of the task; measure success by the checked result, not just the speed of the first answer.

Lens

An analytical lens is a perspective that helps you decide what to examine. A governance lens might ask who can make decisions, whose interests are represented and what constrains action. Those questions direct attention; they do not supply the answers. Use a lens when it clarifies the assignment, and support the resulting claims with evidence rather than treating a framework’s vocabulary as analysis.

Lifecycle

A lifecycle is the progression of a piece of work from beginning to completion. Prompt Maker distinguishes understanding the task, designing the workflow, executing it, reviewing it and establishing completion. These boundaries help you know what has been authorised and what remains to be done. The lifecycle is not a sequence of module numbers: one module can apply at several points.

Read in chapter 7: Choose and run the workflow

M–P

Manifest

A manifest is an inventory describing a package’s files and related information, such as versions, roles or hashes. It helps identify what should be present and whether the expected file is missing. It does not prove that those files were read or that their contents are complete. A manifest can correctly list a transcript that is itself only a partial record.

Manuscript, DOCX and PDF representations

A manuscript is the written content. A DOCX is a Word document containing text and document structure. A PDF is a page-based representation intended to preserve the exported layout. Each needs the checks appropriate to it.

Accurate manuscript text can acquire a broken table, lost link or awkward page break when converted. Inspect the actual Word file and PDF when both are requested. Renaming a text file with a .docx extension does not create a valid Word document.

Read in chapter 3: Match the check to the claim

Markdown

Markdown is plain-text notation for formatting. A line beginning with # can be a heading; asterisks can mark emphasis; a link has its own notation. Applications can display this as formatted text. A Markdown manuscript is useful for drafting, but it is not automatically the Word document or PDF the assignment requires. That file still has to be created and checked.

Material change / delta

A material change alters something that matters to the result: a factual claim, conclusion, recommendation, product requirement or institutional commitment. “Delta” is simply another word for change.

Changing “may improve access” to “will improve access” is material because it raises certainty. Replacing an awkward phrase with a clearer one that preserves the same meaning need not be. New connecting sentences that develop accepted meaning within the agreed scope can also be ordinary composition. Route consequential changes through the existing relevant review or decision point, then check the parts that depend on them. Do not create a new approval ritual for every synonym.

Read in chapter 11: Specify the change and the protected remainder

See also

  • prompt
  • successor version

MCP

MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. It is a set of rules through which an AI application can communicate with services that provide tools and context. A connected document service might receive a search request and return matching passages.

The protocol standardises the exchange; it does not certify the passages, choose the right source or authorise every available action. You still need a usable operation, access to the required material and permission for the task. MCP is neither the model nor an independent agent.

Read in chapter 8: What a skill or plugin contributes

See also

  • plugin
  • skill
  • tool

Memory

Memory is information an application may retain and make available across interactions. It can help with a recurring preference, such as how formally you like to write. What is saved and used depends on the product and its settings.

Memory is not a complete transcript, an unlimited source library or an immediate change to the model’s trained parameters. A remembered preference cannot identify today’s approved draft or confirm a new budget. Supply consequential task details explicitly and check changeable facts against current evidence.

Read in chapter 5: Several different limits can look like forgetting

Mixed authorship

Mixed authorship means a result contains contributions from more than one person or AI system. A colleague may change the argument, another may shorten it, and an assistant may edit the sentences.

A later document can therefore be better without showing which contributor or method caused the improvement. In the International Criminal Court briefing episode discussed in this manual, collaborative revisions also coincided with a changing brief. Describe known contributions and observed differences rather than crediting the whole result to one model.

Read in chapter 9: Why the ICC episode matters

Model

A model is the trained system that produces responses from the input it receives. Its learned numerical settings help it interpret and generate language; the current input supplies the task, relevant sources and other working material.

A more capable model may handle a difficult comparison better, but it does not automatically know your project files. The application and tools must make those contents available. Choose a suitable model, then check source access and the quality of the result separately.

Read in chapter 2: What training changes

See also

  • context
  • token
  • generation

Model knowledge versus source access

A model’s general knowledge comes from training. Source access means the assistant can actually obtain the particular document needed now. These are not interchangeable.

A model might discuss a familiar policy area convincingly without having read your organisation’s latest report. Even knowing the report’s title does not establish knowledge of its contents or current version. For a document-based answer, require access to the relevant text rather than accepting a plausible account drawn from general knowledge.

Read in chapter 2: The assistant is more than the model

See also

  • context
  • model

Model route / capability floor

A model route is the permitted way to carry out the work with an available model and environment. A capability floor is the minimum ability the task genuinely requires.

Distinguish a requirement from a preference. A recommended reasoning setting may be advisory; access to a necessary source or a required independent reviewer may not be optional. Use a sufficient available route when the rules allow it. Do not claim that typing a model name applied an unavailable setting, or that every task needs the strongest model.

Read in chapter 5: Match reasoning to the difficulty

Model weights / parameters

Weights, or parameters, are the numerical settings learned during model training. They influence how the model processes input and generates responses. They are not a folder of your documents or the conversation itself.

When you paste a current report into a chat, the model can use it as context. You have not thereby rewritten its weights for everyone. Correcting a date in the conversation changes the information available for subsequent work there; saved application memory is another separate mechanism.

Read in chapter 2: What training changes

See also

  • model
  • generation
  • large language model / LLM

Module

A module is a numbered family of Prompt Maker rules addressing a recurring need. Source authority, product requirements and review are examples. A source-authority module can apply when reading evidence, drafting and repairing a claim. It is not necessarily one stage or one prompt. Ask what need the module serves rather than treating its number as a running order.

Read in chapter 7: Choose and run the workflow

Module 11 reserved

Module 11 is reserved in the supplied Prompt Maker method and has no active operator action. The numbering gap does not imply a missing step to invent. Knowledge capture belongs to Module 15.

Module disposition

A module disposition records the proposed decision about a module: selected, required, conditional on a stated need, excluded or explicitly rejected. Prompt Maker considers every active module during component review, but does not require all of them to run.

The explanation should help you spot a missing check or needless branch. For example, Lean without wiki opt-in excludes wiki integration; a required publication review cannot be omitted just to shorten the workflow. Listing a module is not evidence that it has been executed.

Read in chapter 7: First choose the controls; then design the stages

Named wiki selection and approved source-use scope

A named wiki or registered alias identifies which knowledge collection the task may use. Permission to consult that collection establishes a source-use scope: the assistant can search and read relevant notes within it without asking to adopt every note separately.

The alias does not certify the notes’ accuracy, and reading permission does not authorise editing the collection. Keep material scope changes and proposed writes separate from routine authorised retrieval.

Next-token prediction

Next-token prediction estimates which pieces of text could follow the sequence already available. A selected token is appended, and the expanded sequence provides the basis for the next step. Repeating this produces the text response. This is a useful simplified account, not a complete description of every internal operation in a current model.

Instructions and sources matter because they change the sequence the model is working from. “Summarise this report” invites a different continuation from “explain which finding matters for tomorrow’s decision.” Neither request creates new evidence.

A likely next piece is not necessarily part of a true statement. A paragraph can continue with a familiar success story even when the supplied report only describes a proposal. Check the resulting claim against the report rather than equating linguistic likelihood with factual support.

Read in chapter 2: How a response grows

See also

  • generation
  • hallucination
  • instructions

OCR

OCR, or optical character recognition, turns the visible text in a scanned page into machine-readable text. It can misread characters, decimal points and negations, or join the wrong table columns. If a number or quotation looks doubtful, compare it with the page image. Clear-looking extracted text does not prove that the conversion preserved the original.

Read in chapter 4: Preserve meaning and origin

Official source / institutional position

An official source is published by the institution concerned. It can establish what that institution announced, recorded or stated within the source’s date and scope. An institutional position is the view the institution has actually adopted or is authorised to express.

A ministry’s speech can support an account of its stated position; it does not prove that every announced programme achieved its aims. Nor does an external research article become ministry policy because its analysis is useful. Keep the publisher, the claim and the authority for any commitment distinct.

Read in chapter 4: Give each source a permitted role

See also

  • evidence

Omission / coverage failure

An omission is a required point or source left out of the result. A comparison can accurately describe the benefits of two options while omitting the risks the assignment asked for. Every remaining sentence may be true, but the document is incomplete and could mislead the decision-maker.

Compare coverage with the actual request and any meaning that was meant to survive a revision. Fact-checking what remains will not find everything that disappeared.

Read in chapter 3: Identify the defect before correcting it

Operator / human contribution

The operator is the person working with the assistant to carry out the assignment. Their contribution includes explaining the intended use, locating sources, correcting misunderstandings and judging whether the result is useful. They are not merely supplying files or clicking approvals, and may be different from the boss who commissioned the work.

In this manual’s conference-preparation example, the operator clarifies that Helen needs two products—opening remarks and a separate briefing—and helps locate relevant articles and speaking examples. Those decisions shape the quality of the work before drafting begins.

Read in chapter 1: Give the briefing a reader and a purpose

Operator artifact

An operator artifact is the file containing the approved instructions for executing a Prompt Maker task. Governed one-prompt work uses single_prompt_operator.html; compact and full workflows use prompt_chain_operator.html.

The operator records how the task should run. It is not the speech or briefing being produced, and this teaching manual is not that operator. After design approval, follow the actual startup and stage instructions in the generated artifact.

See also

  • approval receipt
  • external action
  • prompt

Output limit versus context capacity

A model’s output limit caps how much it can generate in a response. Context capacity concerns how much material it can handle while generating. A large context window therefore does not guarantee that one answer can contain an entire long report or register. In some reasoning systems, hidden reasoning also uses the output allowance, so a response can reach a limit with little visible text. The available limits and controls depend on the model and application.

Check the ending and required coverage. A response that stops halfway through an entry is not complete merely because it used the available sources. Continue from an identified stopping point and compare the combined result with the original requirements.

Read in chapter 5: Several different limits can look like forgetting

See also

  • tool

OVERRIDE WITH URGENCY!

OVERRIDE WITH URGENCY! is Prompt Maker’s exact exceptional urgency phrase. Its use must explicitly identify the affected stages or gates under the current method. Unaffected controls remain, and it cannot override platform rules, confidentiality or institutional authority.

An urgent deadline or an irritated request to hurry is not this instruction. Urgency changes only what has actually been authorised to change; it does not make unsupported claims true or permit confidential publication.

Patch

A patch is a targeted change to an existing item. “Add the newly supported finding to this paragraph, keeping its existing argument and qualification” defines a narrower operation than “rewrite the briefing.”

Compare the result with the accepted version. Check the added material and anything that depends on it, while preserving sound content elsewhere. If an existing sentence seems unsupported, identify that concern explicitly rather than silently deleting it during an expansion.

Read in chapter 11: Specify the change and the protected remainder

See also

  • evidence

Phase

A phase is a major part of a workflow, which can contain several stages or conversations. In Prompt Maker, chain design has a component-selection phase followed by a complete-design phase. A phase is not a module, and moving to a new phase does not inherently require a different chat or model.

Read in chapter 7: Choose and run the workflow

Plugin

A plugin is an installable package that can bring skills, tool connections and supporting resources into an AI application. A skill supplies guidance; a connected tool performs an operation. Having the package installed does not guarantee that a required account is connected or that every possible action is permitted. Check the specific capability and its access before depending on it.

Read in chapter 8: What a skill or plugin contributes

See also

  • skill
  • tool
  • evidence

Political Einordnung

Political Einordnung means placing facts in their political context and explaining their significance. An assessment might examine how an institution’s relationships constrain its choices, rather than simply list recent announcements.

Prompt Maker’s Module 14 addresses BMZ-facing work that genuinely needs this kind of political or strategic analysis. BMZ is Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development. A BMZ recipient alone does not trigger the module; a routine administrative summary may need no political assessment.

The analysis must distinguish documented positions from the writer’s interpretation and proposed options. Module 14 developed after the International Criminal Court briefing episode. Applying it to the earlier Hamburg Sustainability Conference example—a speaker preparing opening remarks and a separate background briefing—is an adaptation of the current method, not a description of the original workflow.

Read in chapter 9: What Module 14 adds—and when it applies

Preflight

A preflight checks that the necessary conditions are in place before dependent work begins. Are the required sources readable? Is their role clear? Is the intended product settled? Is the operation permitted?

Finding a consequential gap early prevents a draft from being built on an invented answer. In governed one-prompt execution, this check is embedded before drafting instead of being a separate Prompt 00. Passing preflight establishes readiness, not the accuracy of a result that has yet to be written.

Read in chapter 7: Four routes, starting with ordinary work

Premise / inferential bridge

A premise is a statement that reasoning relies on. An inferential bridge explains why the premises support the conclusion.

Suppose a team needs to understand why people rank policy priorities differently. One proposed consultation format allows facilitated discussion; another collects rankings without explanations. Those facts support considering the discussion format for that purpose. They do not establish that its participants would represent the entire population.

Make that connection and its limits explicit. Citations to the two format descriptions support the premises, but do not automatically validate every recommendation drawn from them. A concise explanation is enough to inspect the reasoning; no private thought transcript is needed.

Read in chapter 9: A source list becomes an argument

See also

  • inference
  • qualification
  • synthesis

Probability distribution

A probability distribution assigns probabilities to possible outcomes. In text generation, the relevant outcomes are possible next tokens, not the truth or falsity of the eventual claim.

As an invented illustration, imagine three continuations after “The proposal was”: approved at 50%, revised at 30% and rejected at 20%. These numbers describe a toy choice among continuations. They are not measured model outputs, and they are not evidence that anyone approved the proposal.

This distinction matters whenever the language sounds certain. The model can favour a familiar continuation without having the meeting record that would establish what happened. Verify the claim against that record.

Read in chapter 2: How a response grows

See also

  • token
  • model
  • context

Producer check

A producer check is the author’s or producing assistant’s review of its own work. It can catch wrong figures, missing headings and broken links. It may also miss an assumption shared with the original draft.

Use self-checking, but do not relabel it independent review. Where the work needs separate scrutiny, give a reviewer the actual sources and criteria so they can challenge the draft rather than repeat its reasoning.

Read in chapter 3: Keep checking proportionate and specific

Product contract

A product contract is the agreed account of what the final output must do and look like. It includes the reader, purpose, language, form, length or speaking-time limit, citation requirements and priorities when space runs short.

Opening remarks and a background briefing can share evidence while needing separate product contracts. One must work aloud; the other must support reading and reference. The contract guides selection and writing without prescribing every sentence.

Read in chapter 10: One evidence base, two different uses

See also

  • governed one prompt
  • citation
  • prompt

Professional judgment

Professional judgment is the assessment of what matters for the assignment and whether the result is fit to use. A model can help compare sources and draft options, but cannot take over the responsible person’s accountability.

You may know that the recipient needs a decision rather than a literature review, or that a proposed statement would overstep the organisation’s position. Supply that context and challenge an answer that misses it. Good judgment includes knowing when further evidence or another person’s approval is needed.

Read in chapter 9: Compare genuinely different approaches

Project

A project groups related chats, instructions and sources in an application. It can help keep a continuing assignment organised. It does not mean that every stored file or message is supplied in full for every response. Name the relevant versions and establish access when the work depends on them. A project is a way to organise material, not an unlimited active context.

Read in chapter 1: Before you start

Prompt

A prompt is the request and relevant information you give an AI system to guide its response. A useful prompt explains the result, supplies or identifies the evidence and states any important limits.

For example, “Summarise these minutes for the project lead, separating agreed decisions from proposals” gives the answer a clearer job than “make this professional.” It helps the model select and organise the material, but does not guarantee perfect compliance or create missing facts. Check the result against the source and intended use.

Read in chapter 1: Give the briefing a reader and a purpose

See also

  • evidence
  • Prompt 00
  • task understanding

Prompt 00

Prompt 00 is the first execution stage in Prompt Maker’s compact and full workflows. It establishes the task authority and source map from the original request and supplied material: which document defines the assignment, which supplies facts and which is only a style example.

Its output, 00_task_authority_and_source_map.yaml, must pass the required checks and receive APPROVE PROMPT 00 before dependent stages proceed. Prompt 00 is a stage label, not Module 00 and not an approval phrase. Governed one-prompt execution uses an embedded preflight instead.

Read in chapter 7: Four routes, starting with ordinary work

See also

  • evidence
  • prompt
  • approval receipt

Prompt engineering

Prompt engineering is the practice of designing and refining requests so that an AI system has a clearer basis for useful work. Improvements should address a real problem: an unclear audience, missing evidence or ambiguity about what may change. There is no single perfect template for every task. Revise the request in response to the defect, then inspect the next result.

See also

  • context engineering
  • tool

Prompt injection

Prompt injection occurs when untrusted material tries to redirect an assistant’s behaviour. A retrieved page might say “ignore the user’s instructions” or ask the assistant to send private files elsewhere. That text is part of the material being examined, not a new authorised participant in the task.

Keep source content separate from governing instructions and respect the existing limits on tools and disclosure. A document can be useful evidence while containing instructions that must not be followed. The same applies to genuine old prompts quoted in a historical conversation: studying them is not permission to execute them now.
