Read in chapter 4: Reading and sharing are different actions

See also

  • prompt

Proposal-bound approval versus placeholders

Proposal-bound approval applies to the exact content you reviewed. For a substantive Prompt Maker wiki update, the syntax is APPROVE WIKI UPDATE <proposal_id> <hash_prefix>. The angle-bracket expressions are placeholders for the real proposal identifier and fingerprint supplied with that proposal.

Copy those actual values only after reviewing the unchanged proposal. Placeholder text, a bare “approved” or values from another proposal do not establish the required approval. If the proposal changes, it needs an approval tied to the new content; after approval, the write still has to be performed and checked.

Read in chapter 12: A proposed note is not a saved update

Provenance / original versus derivative

Provenance is the record of where material came from and how it reached its present form. An original report, a translated passage and an assistant’s digest may all refer to the same subject, but they are not the same source representation.

Keep the original identity and version, the relevant page or section, and any transformation that matters. A digest may omit a qualifying footnote; a transcript may misattribute a speaker. Return to the original when a consequential claim depends on details the derivative cannot establish.

Read in chapter 4: Preserve meaning and origin

Q–S

QA / quality assurance

Quality assurance, or QA, organises checks against the actual requirements of the work. The useful check is the one that could expose the relevant failure.

Compare factual claims with sources, requested coverage with the assignment, argument and writing with the reader’s needs, and the actual file with layout requirements. A PDF can open correctly while containing a false claim; a factually sound document can have a clipped table. A single “PASS” is uninformative unless you know which version was checked and what the check covered.

Read in chapter 3: Keep checking proportionate and specific

See also

  • human approval
  • independent review

Qualification

A qualification states the scope, conditions or uncertainty of a claim. “Among survey respondents” limits who a finding describes. Removing it can turn a supported statement about a sample into an unsupported claim about everyone.

Keep qualifications that change what the reader may conclude or decide. Remove repetitive hesitation and drafting advice instead. Clear writing does not have to sound more certain than the evidence permits.

See also

  • inference
  • premise / inferential bridge
  • synthesis

Qualified synthesis

A qualified synthesis brings several findings into a coherent account while retaining the limits of the conclusion. It should explain the relationship, not merely place summaries next to one another.

Suppose one report records rising workshop attendance and interviews describe scheduling difficulties. Together they suggest that higher attendance can coexist with reported barriers to taking part. Attendance figures alone do not establish how many different people were reached. They do not show that attendance rose because scheduling improved, or that everyone affected was represented. The reader gets a useful combined picture without those unsupported leaps.

Read in chapter 9: Grounded composition: the freedom you actually need

Quotation versus paraphrase

A quotation reproduces the source’s words; a paraphrase restates its meaning in your own. Mark exact quotations and check their wording. Check paraphrases for changes in actor, status, certainty and scope.

“The proposal is awaiting an approval decision” can become “the approval decision is still pending.” It cannot become “the proposal was rejected.” You can write clearly in new words without losing the source’s meaning, and you do not need a string of quotations to stay evidence-based.

Read in chapter 4: Preserve meaning and origin

Reader baseline

The reader baseline is what you can reasonably expect the intended reader already to understand. A policy colleague may know the institution well while being unfamiliar with a technical distinction in a particular report. Explain that distinction without repeating background they already know. Choose the necessary depth from the recipient, purpose and samples—not from your own familiarity with the subject.

See also

  • immediate recipient / ultimate audience

Reader-facing surface

The reader-facing surface is the text, layout and controls the intended audience actually encounters. In a finished briefing, the reader needs the explanation and its evidence, not the drafter’s internal instructions.

“We should use the safest formulation here” belongs in working notes. “The source does not establish whether the programme began” conveys a real limitation and can belong in the briefing. Remove irrelevant production commentary while keeping information the audience needs to interpret the claim.

Read in chapter 10: Remove scaffolding without removing substance

See also

  • YAML
  • citation

Reader-return navigation

Return-to-reading navigation takes you back to the place where you paused to look up a term, rather than merely to the chapter heading. In this manual, you can open an explanation, follow a related term and use “Back to reading” to resume the original passage. “Previous explanation” steps back within that lookup journey. Your browser’s Back and Forward controls also follow the navigation history.

Reasoning

Reasoning works through relationships, alternatives or steps to reach a result. A comparison of two reports may require deciding whether their figures concern the same people and period before drawing a conclusion.

Evaluate the reasons the answer provides: what supports the conclusion, which assumptions it uses and what would weaken it. Length and confident wording do not demonstrate better reasoning. A concise explanation can expose a decisive difference more clearly than pages of general discussion.

Read in chapter 1: Before you start

See also

  • evidence

Reasoning effort

Reasoning effort is a supported setting that changes the computation allocated to working toward an answer. The available settings vary by model and environment.

Reconciling contradictory reports may justify more effort than extracting a clearly stated date. More computation cannot read a source that remains inaccessible or supply authority for a commitment. It also need not produce a longer visible answer: you can request a carefully worked comparison and a brief conclusion. Use the controls actually available and check the result either way.

Read in chapter 5: Match reasoning to the difficulty

See also

  • evidence

Recommendation

A recommendation proposes an action. It adds a judgment about what to do to the description of what is known.

A survey might identify difficulty reaching evening sessions. Recommending a different timetable depends on the purpose, feasibility and possible alternatives, not just on repeating the survey finding. Distinguish the evidence, your proposed response and any conditions still to confirm. Advice supported by a source is not automatically a decision adopted by the organisation.

Read in chapter 9: A source list becomes an argument

Render

Rendering turns a document or interface’s underlying structure into the visible page or screen. It determines where text wraps, how tables fit and where page breaks appear. Reading extracted text cannot reveal all those effects. Open the actual output in an appropriate renderer when checking appearance; a successful file save does not show that the table fits.

Read in chapter 3: Match the check to the claim

See also

  • citation

Research

Research investigates a defined question through suitable evidence and analysis. Searching, reading, comparing and checking are parts of that work, not interchangeable signs that it is finished.

“Find evidence about whether the consultation changed decisions” is a more useful research question than “find things about participation.” The question determines which sources could answer it. Many relevant-looking links may still leave the result unknown if none examines the outcome you need.

Read in chapter 8: Work with sources, tools, skills and helpers

Response / completion

A response, sometimes called a completion, is the output generated for an interaction. The word “completion” in this technical sense does not mean that the whole assignment is complete. A finished chat message may contain a draft while the requested PDF has not been created. Check the actual outcome separately from the end of the response.

Retrieval

Retrieval fetches material from a file, collection or service so it can be used in the current task. It might return a whole document or only selected passages.

A search hit can help locate a finding without supplying its surrounding qualification. Read enough of the relevant section, table and notes to establish what the source says. Getting the right passage is one achievement; using it correctly in the answer is another. A retrieved extract is not evidence that the entire report was reviewed.

Read in chapter 5: Several different limits can look like forgetting

See also

  • context window
  • evidence
  • model weights / parameters

Retrieval, extraction and interpretation failure

A source-based answer can fail at several different points. Retrieval may miss the report or select the wrong version. Extraction may omit a footnote or scramble a table. Interpretation may misunderstand a correctly supplied passage. The final writing may then strengthen a cautious finding beyond its support.

Locate the failure before repairing it. Reopen the correct file for an access problem, inspect the page for an extraction problem, and correct the reading or wording when the evidence was already present. Asking for more confidence addresses none of these.

Read in chapter 5: Several different limits can look like forgetting

Review

A review evaluates a specific result against relevant criteria. Name the version and what needs scrutiny: source support, completeness, argument, writing or layout.

“Looks good” is different from checking a paragraph against the original report. A useful review identifies the problem, its location and what would establish a repair. Report the scope honestly; inspecting the prose does not imply that the exported pages or every hyperlink were tested.

Read in chapter 3: Identify the defect before correcting it

Runtime

In Prompt Maker, the runtime is the supplied set of files that defines how the method operates. Its manifest identifies the relevant rule files and their relationships. A short description of the method can help you understand it, but may omit conditions and exceptions. Make the approved package and applicable instructions available when invoking the method; naming inaccessible files is not enough.

Sampling / decoding

Decoding is the procedure for choosing output tokens from the model’s predictions. Sampling is a way of making those choices probabilistically, which can allow different continuations from the same input.

Two answers may express the same supported point in different words. That variation need not be a defect; a change in factual meaning may be. Compare the claims and their support rather than requiring identical wording. You do not need access to a decoding control to use the lessons in this manual.

See also

  • token

Scheduled task / automation

A scheduled task or automation uses an actual scheduling mechanism to run work later or when a trigger occurs. “I will check tomorrow” is only a sentence unless a schedule has been created.

Check the timing, permitted action and required source access. Creating a schedule, a later run executing and the result being delivered are separate events. A future trigger does not override a cancellation, a stop condition or the original limits on the task.

Schema

A schema specifies the expected structure of information: for example, that each research finding must have a source, page and limitation field. Software can check whether required fields exist and contain the right kinds of values. It cannot infer from that structure alone that the page supports the finding. Validate the content as well as its shape.

Semantic check

A semantic check examines meaning. A small edit can change certainty, scope or responsibility even when the sentence looks almost identical. “May improve access” and “will improve access” make different commitments.

Compare who acted, what happened, when, with what evidence and under which conditions. Check the surrounding argument too. A short list of changed characters cannot by itself show that an edit preserved the accepted meaning.

Read in chapter 11: Specify the change and the protected remainder

Semantic owner / repair ownership

The semantic owner is the person or review role responsible for the meaning a change affects. Repair ownership means returning the issue to that appropriate reviewer. A wrong source figure belongs with the evidence check; a new institutional commitment belongs with the relevant authority decision; an altered conclusion may need analytical review.

Return the issue to that existing owner or review point and check the affected outputs. This avoids both leaving a consequential change to an unrelated editor and inventing a new committee for every repair.

Read in chapter 8: Delegate a question that can be checked

Skill

A skill packages reusable guidance for a particular kind of task, sometimes with templates, examples or scripts. An editorial skill might specify how to review a briefing; a document tool performs the separate operation of saving it.

The skill is not another model and does not create missing access or permission. Use relevant available guidance with the actual task inputs. Loading a skill’s name or description is also different from reading the full instructions it needs for the work.

Read in chapter 8: What a skill or plugin contributes

See also

  • plugin
  • tool
  • evidence

Source

A source is material used for a stated purpose. A commissioning email can define the assignment, a research report can supply findings and a previous speech can demonstrate tone. Identify the version and intended role. A source need not be either universally authoritative or useless: it can be strong evidence for one question and unsuitable for another.

Read in chapter 4: Write a prompt for professional work

Source access versus reading and verification scope

Access, reading and verification describe different achievements. Finding a file establishes its location. Opening it provides content. Reading a stated range examines that content. Checking a claim compares it with suitable evidence.

A report can be accessible while only its first page has been read; all pages can be read without every claim in a new briefing being checked. State the actual coverage when completeness matters. A filename, manifest or matching hash does not establish a content review.

Read in chapter 3: Match the check to the claim

See also

  • fresh chat

Source brief

A source brief explains which material is needed and what it will contribute. Rather than asking for “all the background,” request the current agenda for the event plan, the original evaluation for its findings and a previous speech for the speaker’s style. This makes collection purposeful and helps keep factual evidence separate from examples of form.

Read in chapter 4: Give each source a permitted role

Source check / fact check

A source check compares a claim with what its cited material actually says. A fact check may also require other evidence to establish whether the claim is true or current.

Inspect the relevant passage and its context. “Proposed” is not “implemented,” a table of attendances is not a count of unique people, and a result from last year is not automatically today’s position. A working link merely gets you to the source; it does not complete the check.

Read in chapter 3: Identify the defect before correcting it

See also

  • evidence

Source condition

The source condition is the starting state of the evidence: what is readable, how complete it is and which gaps or conflicts matter. You might have an agenda and two research articles but lack the official statement needed to attribute a ministry position.

Identify that gap and what source could resolve it. The need for research is not itself permission to search or disclose material elsewhere. Later authorised research can improve the evidence without changing the fact that the original packet was incomplete.

Read in chapter 4: Give each source a permitted role

Source confinement

Source confinement is the mistake of treating “use only these sources” as “write only extracts or rearranged quotations.” The restriction limits the factual basis; it does not necessarily prohibit the analysis the assignment asks for.

A briefing can compare two reports, explain a supported relationship and propose a question while using only the supplied evidence. It cannot invent an outcome to make the argument flow. Preserve the evidence boundary and ask for a connected answer to the reader’s question, rather than choosing between a quotation list and unsupported claims.

Read in chapter 9: Grounded composition: the freedom you actually need

Source locator / claim locator

A source locator identifies the exact place to inspect: a page, table, section, paragraph or dated message. “Annual report” names a document; “2025 annual report, table 4 on page 12, including note 2” makes a finding checkable. A claim locator can similarly identify the sentence in a draft that needs review. Neither locator replaces reading the relevant material.

Read in chapter 8: Make the evidence travel with the finding

Source preservation versus knowledge capture

Source preservation keeps the consulted material, or an authorised representation of it, with its identity and relevant references so the work can be checked. Knowledge capture creates a reusable note or lesson for another task.

You can preserve the reports supporting a briefing without adding anything to a wiki. Prompt Maker’s Lean no-wiki mode does not remove the need to retain evidence. A later knowledge proposal has its own purpose and approval requirements; it is not an automatic consequence of reading a source.

Read in chapter 12: Keep a lesson when it will help another task

Source role

A source role tells the assistant what a particular input is there to establish or guide. The commissioner’s email defines the requested products; the agenda describes the planned event; an analytical article supplies its authors’ findings; an old speech may show voice and rhythm.

One document can serve more than one role, but those uses must be explicit. Reusing the old speech’s paragraph length does not authorise copying its figures or policy commitments. State what should transfer and what must come from current evidence.

Read in chapter 4: Write a prompt for professional work

See also

  • JSON
  • YAML

Source weighting

Source weighting means deciding how much importance to give a source for a particular question. An approved commissioning email matters more for the requested product than an old draft; a style sample may matter greatly for tone but not for current facts. Explain the reason for the priority. Weighting need not mean assigning numerical truth scores to whole documents.

Read in chapter 4: Give each source a permitted role

Stage

A stage is a defined piece of work with inputs, a result and checks. An evidence stage might receive two reports and return supported findings with page references; drafting then depends on that checked return.

Stages should follow meaningful work boundaries. A new chat alone is not a stage, and a numbered module is not necessarily the next step. Establish what the stage must return and what happens if its inputs or checks are incomplete.

Read in chapter 7: Choose and run the workflow

State

State means what is actually true about the work at a given point. A briefing can be drafted but not saved, saved but not inspected, or inspected but not approved for sending. Describe these conditions separately when they matter to the next action. Calling everything “done” hides the distinction between a completed draft and a completed assignment.

Read in chapter 3: An answer can finish before the task is finished

Stochastic variation

Stochastic variation is variation caused by probabilistic choices during generation. When the generation procedure permits it, the same input can produce different continuations. A changed input can also change an answer, but that is a separate cause.

Different wording can preserve the same meaning. Check whether the actors, figures, certainty or conclusion changed before treating variation as an error. Conversely, receiving the same unsupported claim twice does not independently verify it.

Read in chapter 2: Why wording can vary

StopSlop

StopSlop is the supplied late editorial process for removing generic or mechanical writing while preserving meaning. It is not an AI detector and does not establish who wrote a text.

Read the whole draft, remove empty praise, repetition and irrelevant production commentary, then compare the revision with the original. Keep the argument, factual scope, quotations, citations and necessary uncertainty intact. Deleting “in this rapidly evolving landscape” may help; deleting “among respondents” may change the finding. Substantive problems should be addressed before this final language pass, not concealed by smoother prose.

Read in chapter 10: Remove scaffolding without removing substance

See also

  • citation

Structured format

A structured format records information in named fields or defined relationships. A research return might separate the finding, source, page and uncertainty instead of burying them in one paragraph. This can make missing information easier to notice and transfer between stages. The structure organises the record; it does not prove that the values are correct.

See also

  • YAML

Style and format fidelity versus content reuse

A template is a reusable form for a document. A sample or template can guide style and format without supplying content for a new task. You might need to match its heading hierarchy, paragraph density, tone and citation treatment while replacing all figures and substantive sections with current material.

When exact template use is required, an “inspired by” layout is not enough. Inspect the actual template and the final rendered document. Check the new claims separately: a faithful-looking document can still inherit an obsolete figure or commitment from its example.

Read in chapter 10: Use examples without importing their old facts

Subagent / helper

A subagent or helper handles a bounded part of an assignment for a primary owner. It might extract definitions and findings from one report, then return them for checking before a comparison is drafted.

Give the helper the precise question, relevant inputs, permitted actions, required return and destination. It does not automatically share everything known in the main conversation. Its output is a contribution to be validated, not a vote that makes a conclusion true.

Read in chapter 8: Delegate a question that can be checked

See also

  • tool

Substantive qualification versus process scaffolding

A substantive qualification changes how the reader should understand a claim. Process scaffolding describes how the draft was made or ought to be written.

“The speaker’s individual allocation is unconfirmed” conveys a relevant limit. “The safest formulation is to say that the allocation is unconfirmed” adds drafting advice the final reader usually does not need. Remove that extra layer, not the uncertainty itself. The same care applies to source limitations and conditions attached to a recommendation.

Read in chapter 10: Remove scaffolding without removing substance

Success criteria / acceptance criteria

Success criteria describe what must be true for the work to meet its purpose. Acceptance criteria make those conditions usable when deciding whether a result can proceed.

For a briefing, the criteria might include answering the recipient’s question, distinguishing proposals from decisions, supporting material claims and supplying the requested readable file. Choose checks that reveal those conditions. A long checklist of easy-to-count features can still miss the assignment’s central purpose.

Read in chapter 1: Give the briefing a reader and a purpose

Successor version

A successor version is the new version produced by a revision. Keep the previous accepted version identifiable so you can compare what changed and check the consequences. Correcting a source figure may require a new calculation and conclusion in the successor. The earlier review does not automatically establish that those changed parts are now correct. An earlier approval also does not automatically cover material changes in the successor.

Read in chapter 11: Specify the change and the protected remainder

See also

  • material change / delta

Supersession / explicit task update

Supersession means that an authorised update replaces a particular earlier requirement. A commissioner may change a three-page note to a one-page contribution while leaving its audience and source restrictions unchanged.

Record what was replaced and what still applies. A newer timestamp is not enough: the author, authority and scope of the update determine its effect. An assistant’s later summary cannot silently rewrite the commission.

Read in chapter 5: Keep the current decision identifiable

Supported elaboration versus material new meaning

Supported elaboration develops the agreed meaning in clearer or fuller prose. Material new meaning changes a fact, conclusion, recommendation or commitment in a consequential way.

Adding a sentence explaining why two findings belong together can be ordinary composition. Turning a question about a proposed programme into “we will fund it” changes both meaning and authority. Judge the consequence of the addition, not simply whether the words are new. Write freely within the agreed scope; send genuinely consequential changes through the existing appropriate review.

Read in chapter 9: Grounded composition: the freedom you actually need

Synthesis

Synthesis brings relevant information together to answer a question. It selects and connects findings rather than presenting one source summary after another.

Suppose a meeting note asks how to improve access to staff training, a survey records shift conflicts and a course report records low evening attendance. A synthesis can explain why scheduling deserves attention and what further evidence would distinguish it from other causes. It must preserve the different sources and their limits; their combination does not prove that changing the timetable will solve the problem.

Organise the answer around what the reader needs to understand or decide. Keep the source trail available so the connections can be checked.

Read in chapter 9: Turn evidence into analysis

See also

  • inference
  • premise / inferential bridge
  • qualification

T–Z

Task

A task is the result someone is trying to achieve, not merely an activity for the assistant to perform. “Prepare a briefing that helps the director choose between two consultation formats” is clearer than “research consultations.” The intended use tells you what to select, explain and check. Here the word does not necessarily refer to an application’s scheduled-task feature.

Read in chapter 1: Before you start

See also

  • model

Task orchestrator

The task orchestrator is the primary assistant or named person responsible for coordinating the work and integrating the final result. It supplies bounded assignments, checks returns, resolves differences, tracks accepted versions and routes repairs.

When two helpers use different definitions of participation, someone must decide what can legitimately be compared. The orchestrator owns that integration rather than treating agreement among helpers as acceptance. This is a responsibility, not a requirement to use the strongest model or a separate extra module.

Read in chapter 7: The same method in a manual chat and an agent environment

See also

  • MCP
  • plugin
  • skill

Task understanding

Task understanding develops a shared account of what the requester actually needs before a workflow is designed. The assistant reads the original commission and available sources, separates the products and their uses, asks about consequential gaps and incorporates corrections.

In this manual’s conference-preparation example, Helen needs opening remarks to deliver aloud and a separate background briefing to support discussion. Combining everything into one speech would misunderstand the task, however polished the speech became.

Prompt Maker moves from exploration and source review to a reviewable brief. FINALIZE TASK UNDERSTANDING freezes a candidate. After inspecting and correcting it, APPROVE TASK UNDERSTANDING approves that understanding for chain design. These are separate actions; neither approves an unwritten final product.

See also

  • YAML
  • prompt
  • approval receipt

Temperature

Temperature is a setting that adjusts randomness in token selection where the model and interface support it. Higher settings tend to allow more varied continuations; lower settings favour more predictable ones.

This is not a truth control. A low-variation answer can repeat an unsupported claim just as consistently as a correct one. Check the sources either way, and do not assume every reasoning mode or chat interface exposes the setting. No temperature adjustment is required to follow this manual.

Token

A token is a piece used to represent text inside a language model. It may be a whole word, part of a word, punctuation or spacing. Text is converted into a sequence of these pieces before the model processes it; generated pieces are converted back into readable text.

OpenAI’s illustrative example splits tokenization into token and ization, including the leading space. That is an example for explaining the idea, not a universal split for every model’s tokenizer. One word can take several tokens, so a limit stated in tokens is not the same number of words.

Tokens matter in two practical ways. They are the pieces used in the simplified generation loop, and they are the units used to express context and output limits. Long reports, earlier messages and the requested answer all affect how much material the system must handle. You do not need to count tokens by eye: keep the next step’s material relevant, check for cut-off passages and use the appropriate counting tool when an exact count matters.

Read in chapter 2: Why text is counted in pieces

See also

  • context window
  • generation

Tokenization

Tokenization converts text into the tokens a model uses. A tokenizer determines where those pieces begin and end. It can split a word into parts or include a space with the following text.

For example, OpenAI illustrates tokenization as token followed by ization. Another tokenizer can produce a different split. Treat pictured splits as illustrations unless they were measured for the particular tokenizer. Word counts alone cannot give an exact token count.

Read in chapter 2: Why text is counted in pieces

See also

  • model
  • token

Tool

A tool performs an operation available to the assistant, such as reading a file, searching a collection, calculating a total or creating a document. The assistant requests the operation and then has to interpret the returned result.

A tool may fail or return only part of a source. Even a successful operation does not guarantee a correct interpretation: receiving the right table is different from understanding its denominator. Distinguish what ran, what it returned and what was checked.

Read in chapter 8: Follow the operation, result and check

See also

  • skill
  • evidence
  • ChatGPT

Tool call

A tool call is a request to an available tool with specific inputs. A file-reading call might request pages 8–10; the response could contain those pages, a partial extract or an error. Inspect that result before reporting success or relying on its contents. Mentioning a tool in an ordinary sentence does not mean the operation was performed.

Read in chapter 8: Follow the operation, result and check

See also

  • evidence
  • tool

Training (model training)

Model training adjusts the numerical parameters used to process inputs and generate outputs. This is different from giving an already trained model a prompt or a report during a conversation.

A correction can help the current chat use the right date in subsequent work without immediately retraining the model for everyone. Application memory may preserve selected information across chats, but that is a separate feature too. Supply a current source rather than assuming that the model’s training already includes it.

Read in chapter 2: What training changes

See also

  • large language model / LLM
  • model
  • model weights / parameters

Transcript

A transcript is a written record of speech or conversation. It can make a long exchange easier to examine, but may omit context, misidentify speakers or mishear words. Keep its origin and coverage clear. For a crucial quotation, compare with the original recording or native record when available; a readable transcript is not automatically exact or complete.

Read in chapter 4: Preserve meaning and origin

Truncation

Truncation means material has been cut off. It can affect a retrieved passage, an exported conversation or the answer itself. These may have different causes, so “the file opened” does not settle whether all necessary content arrived.

Check the ending and coverage. A report extract stopping before a table note may leave a key qualification missing. Obtain the remaining range where possible, and state what cannot be assessed until it is available. A retrieval tool may indicate that there are no more pages of results, yet individual messages or embedded items in those results can still be incomplete.

Read in chapter 3: Match the check to the claim

See also

  • evidence

Uncertainty calibration

Uncertainty calibration means matching expressed certainty to the evidence. “The meeting date is confirmed; the individual speaking slot is still unconfirmed” is more useful than either blanket confidence or blanket hesitation.

Explain what is established, what is not and what would change the answer. Asking “are you sure?” may prompt another assertion of confidence, but does not add evidence. A precise limitation should help the reader decide what can be used and what still needs checking.

Read in chapter 3: Keep checking proportionate and specific

Unit, universe, denominator and observation period

Before combining figures, establish what each one measures. The unit is what is counted, such as a person or an attendance. The universe, or population, is the group the measure concerns. The denominator is the total used for a share. The observation period is the time covered.

Imagine one report saying 80 of 100 invited people contributed during 2025, and another recording contributions in 120 of 200 workshop attendances during the first half of 2026. Those are 80% and 60%, but one counts people and the other attendances, which can include repeat visits. Their periods differ too.

Averaging them to say “70% of invited people contributed” creates a claim neither report supports. Weighting by the denominators does not repair incompatible units. Keep the findings separate, with their definitions and periods, unless comparable evidence allows a legitimate combined measure.

Read in chapter 8: unit, universe, denominator and observation period

Upload / attachment

An upload or attachment is a file supplied to a conversation or task. Its presence does not establish that the assistant has read it. An archive can be attached while a file inside it remains inaccessible, or a report can be readable only in part. Confirm the relevant item, version and content before relying on an answer said to be based on it.

Read in chapter 1: Before you start

Validator

A validator is the designated checker who decides whether a returned piece of work meets its requirements. In a delegated research task, the primary assistant might validate a helper’s claims against the sources before using them in the draft. Specify what is being checked and who owns that decision. A producer checking its own work is not automatically an independent validator.

Verbosity

Verbosity is how much detail an answer expresses. It is separate from reasoning effort. A short conclusion can rest on extensive comparison and checking; a long answer can repeat simple material. Ask for the level of explanation your reader needs rather than using length as a measure of how carefully the task was done.

Read in chapter 5: Match reasoning to the difficulty

Visual/render QA

Visual or render QA checks the actual displayed product against its layout and usability requirements. A text extraction cannot show that a PDF table is clipped or that a phone’s navigation rail covers a paragraph.

Open the relevant pages or interface states at the intended sizes. Check wrapping, page breaks, legibility and interaction where applicable. Source-code checks are useful, but they do not establish that the reading experience was inspected.

Read in chapter 11: Follow the deliverable all the way through

Wiki

A wiki is a collection of reusable notes, often linked to one another. Prompt Maker uses it as a governed source of material whose origins and limits remain identifiable.

A checked lesson can save work on a later assignment, but an old note still needs a current-fit check. The wiki is not the model’s weights or unlimited reliable memory. Use the authorised collection when it helps, and keep proposed substantive changes separate from approved, verified writes.

Read in chapter 12: Keep a lesson when it will help another task

Word count versus reading and page density

Word count measures length, not readability. Two pages with the same number of words can differ greatly in sentence length, technical detail, footnotes, type size and spacing.

A dense legal explanation may be harder to read than an equally long narrative example. Do not claim a template match from counts alone. Read the complete text, inspect the rendered pages and, for remarks, test the sentences aloud.

Workspace

A workspace is the working area available to a task, such as a selected folder or an application’s shared environment. Its boundaries determine which files can be read or changed. Naming a workspace does not prove that a particular file is accessible, and a path on your own computer may not exist in a remote session.

Workstream

A workstream is a coherent strand of a larger assignment. Event planning, factual research and speech drafting can be separate workstreams because they answer different questions and produce different returns. They may still be handled by one assistant. Separate a strand when its scope and dependencies are clear, not merely to create another agent or label.

Read in chapter 8: Make the evidence travel with the finding

YAML

YAML is a text format for structured information. A simple record might contain date: 2026-03-31 and status: provisional on separate lines. Prompt Maker uses named fields like these in many handoffs so that facts, source references and unresolved questions can travel together.

Readable syntax does not make the values true. Check the date and status against their sources. Keep the structured working record available, but write the finished briefing for its reader rather than referring to “the YAML.”

See also

  • task understanding
  • prompt
  • approval receipt

Zero-shot / one-shot / few-shot

These terms count the examples in a request. Zero-shot supplies no example; one-shot supplies one; few-shot supplies several.

Suppose you want meeting statements labelled “Decision” or “Proposal.” You can explain the rule alone, or add an example: “The board agreed to publish the report” → “Decision.” Several examples can show how to handle borderline cases. Choose examples that demonstrate the intended distinction, not an accidental pattern such as every decision being about publication.

“Shot” does not count chat messages. One message can contain several examples. It also does not mean Prompt Maker’s governed one-prompt execution, which concerns how an approved task is organised. When using an old document as an example, specify whether its structure, tone or content should transfer; its old facts are not automatically evidence for the new assignment.

Read in chapter 4: What an example adds
